In a recent development, the paintings look loose, imperfect, handmade, at a moment when image models produce perfect (statistically average) pictures. My guess is that this contrast is a massive part of why the video went viral. It reminded me of the early days of generative AI art, when the point was to explore the medium. DeepDream (2015) was a debugging tool that people turned into art, works like Edmond de Belamy (2018) came from artists probing what a GAN could do, and artists like Mario Klingemann spent those years making dreamy portraits with neural networks.

Sources indicate that this project feels closer to those early days. In his thesis, Surya describes the path that led here. He started by prompting text-to-image models, where the prompt is the only lever you can pull, and more detail buys more control only up to a point. Training the model itself goes further. The other half of the idea is the medium. The model writes a program of about 150 lines of JavaScript that paints the image. That model output is code. You can read it, edit it and run it again, and the decision behind each brushstroke is visible. And the style comes from a restriction where the model is only allowed ten of the library's methods. More on that below.

In that same period, Anna Ridler photographed thousands of tulips, hand-labelled every one, exhibited the dataset itself as the artwork, and later trained a model on it. I found her work through the references AI agents brought back while building this project and loved it because this project does something very similar by curating a set of images by hand, and then training against them.

Sources indicate that most of the recent RL work on language models uses rewards you can verify. For example, math problems with a known answer, code that passes tests, or graders that are right or wrong and cheap to run. This project is closer to the older exception, RLHF, where the model learns a reward model from human preferences.

In a recent development, here the reward is aesthetic preference. There is no correct answer. The real question of the project is whether you can do RL over taste.

The reward, as his blog defines it and as the RL environment I built implements it:.

HPSv3 is an open 7B preference model. Give it an image and a text description, and it returns a score for how much a person would prefer that image. It was trained on a large set of human choices between pairs of images, so its score is an average of many people's taste. The pairwise judge is Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct, a general vision model called through HF Inference Providers. The pairwise judge sees the candidate painting next to four references randomly selected from the pool, guided by a written description of what to weigh (bleeds, translucent washes, soft edges), each comparison in both presentation orders, and its score is the share of comparisons the candidate wins. Its only standard is the pool, so its score is my taste, as encoded in those ratings.

According to recent reports, those are the weights Narreddi converged on. The pool defines taste here. That moves the work from tuning hyperparameters to building the set that decides what is beautiful.

Sources indicate that I trained three runs with this reward. They differ only in how the weight splits between the two model judges:.

I started with hps-only to validate that the pipeline could learn at all. Once the reward was going up and the metrics were healthy, there was no reason to run it longer, so I introduced the two longer runs instead. The question that the longer runs ask is how much of HPSv3's power can you hand to the pairwise judge? The more weight the judge carries, the more the reward means my taste instead of everyone's, and the harder it should be to climb. Incidentally, if you push it far enough or your style is too far from the average, the model could stop entirely.

Fortunately, it did not stop and both runs with the pairwise judge on learned too. The hand-rated pool can steer the policy, at least as far as the metrics and the final paintings show. The numbers are below.

In a recent development, disclaimer. If we use a frontier model, it can already generate the JavaScript code that paints watercolour from a prompt. That's the starting point. The work here is about teaching a smaller model to do it combined with a person's own artistic preferences.

The environment wraps everything that sits between the model and the reward, including the JavaScript library that the model uses for painting, the system prompt that restricts it, the headless Chromium that renders each sketch, and the gate that rejects cheats.

The library does more of the work than it seems. p5.brush, by @acamposuribe, simulates a medium rather than drawing shapes: pigment bleeds past the edges of a fill, paper has texture, strokes have mass, flow fields drag brushwork around. When the model calls brush.fillBleed(0.25) it is deciding how far the ink runs.

Note. The author of p5.brush had been trying to teach a machine to paint long before any of this. In 2022 he made a generative art series that hides a diary about teaching p5.js to draw like a child: "It is barely able to use the crayons [...] It cannot follow simple commands. I'm done for today, very infuriating." The series was meant to have three pieces, and he made two. When Surya's video went viral, he quoted it, sharing that diary and saying this work is the third piece arriving on its own.

In a recent development, p5.brush exposes 47 methods. The prompt allows 10: scaleBrushes, noStroke, fill, noFill, fillBleed, fillTexture, beginShape, vertex, endShape and circle. What the other thirty-seven add, lines, hatching, custom brushes, would break the watercolour look. With these ten the model can only paint filled shapes, and the library adds the bleed to every one of them.

In a recent development, his blog post saved me a lot of time I could have wasted iterating on the prompt. A long API reference makes the model invent methods that do not exist, and his 200 GEPA iterations converged on a strict allowlist with no documentation. I saw the same failures and wrote the allowlist by hand. My only addition to that recipe is one sentence: paint each petal two or three times, a big pass first and a smaller, more opaque one inside it. This small change made my outputs a lot more colorful.

Recent findings suggest that note. If it's the first time you hear about GEPA, it is an automatic prompt optimizer. A language model reflects in plain words on where the current prompt failed and proposes a better one, and the loop repeats.

It has been revealed that the gate is the final piece. The sketch has to compile, use the library instead of direct p5 calls, put real pigment on the canvas, and not try to trick the scorer, for example by writing text on the canvas.

The pool consists of 178 paintings divided into two tiers based on my personal preferences, love and okay. All of them are actually generated by a model. Four open-weight models, called through Inference Providers, wrote p5.brush sketches, each one working from a real, openly licensed photo of a hibiscus from iNaturalist. A vision model gave written feedback on every sketch, over three refinement iterations. Every final render was then rated one at a time, by me, and 178 made the cut.

Industry observers note that here I chose four different families of models to test their different styles. These four were the open models that produced a valid sketch every time in a quick reliability check, and two other candidates were dropped for failing it. If you want to produce your own pool, you might choose others.

Recent findings suggest that the tiers do real work in the reward. When the pairwise judge draws four references, half come from love and half from okay, so the policy always faces some rivals it can sometimes beat, and a win pays the same against either tier. This is one of my few deliberate changes: the original compares against its top tier only, and I kept the easier tier in the draw so a weak early policy still gets signal.

Sources indicate that no human-made painting is in there, which is a real limitation. p5.brush is a niche library, and the human work that exists in it with accessible code is a handful of pieces, nowhere near what a training corpus would need, as his blog also notes.

The interesting idea here, as I've already discussed previously, is that the model will learn to imitate what the pool contains. If we point the environment at a different dataset, the reward would automatically change without touching a single line of code. For the dataset I generated and openly share, I also include the source sketch.

It has been revealed that if we look closer at the judges, the two of them answer different questions. HPSv3 decides whether it is a flower, and the pairwise judge decides whether it is well painted in the style I chose.

Before anything worked, there was a long stretch of flat reward curves. If you've tried to reproduce a research paper/blog without open artifacts, you probably can relate. Every run tested what I thought was a reasonable theory about what was wrong. A run takes a lot of time, so I queued the next one while still going through the last one's results. As always, starting from something easier that works and then building on top of that was the answer. A simple control task, with no browser and no judges, was the first attempt that learned, and the reason was that my learning rate was just too low.

Another change that cost me time to find was adjusting the LoRA parameters correctly. The usual target_modules list assumes a dense model, and Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B is a mixture of experts that names most of its projections differently, so the adapter was training ten layers out of forty. I solved this by changing it to all-linear, which reaches every linear layer. The routed experts in this architecture are fused tensors that even all-linear leaves frozen, but everything else gets an adapter, and that was enough to learn.

The fix was four changes in TRL's GRPOTrainer:.

These four changes unlocked the first successful run (hps-only), with the reward clearly improving.

With that configuration, all three runs learn. Both judge runs were rolled out for 200 steps and stopped at 110, with the reward still climbing slowly. A step takes fifteen to eighteen minutes, and the comparison between mixes was already stable, so I stopped both to save compute. Mean group reward over the first and final third of each run:.

The three curves line up with how much weight my taste carries. The more the judge weighs, the lower the start and the noisier the climb. judge-led spent its first thirty steps nearly flat before it moved. It is the same move that solved the debugging. Shrink the problem until something learns, then add the hard parts back one at a time.

The pairwise judge term itself climbed in the two runs that used it. The model wins more comparisons against the pool as training advances, which is the claim hps-only could not make. No group in any run collapsed to identical rewards, the GRPO failure mode that kills the gradient. For the curious, the per-metric curves (HPSv3, paint coverage, entropy) are in the repository as CSV.

The full launch command, the hardware and the two environment variables that turn this into the other two runs are in the recipe.

In every run, the first thing the model learned was to stop producing bad paintings, the near-blank canvases and shapeless washes that score under 0.3 in total reward. In hps-only, three quarters of the rise in the group mean comes from bad paintings becoming rare. In the judge runs the collapse is even steeper: rollouts under 0.3 fall from 99 to 16 across judge-led's thirds, and from 37 to 4 in hps-led.

In a recent development, this is why the obvious visual, the best painting of each step, demonstrates almost no difference in hps-only. It moves +0.034 across the run while the median moves +0.155. The learning is visible in the middle of the distribution.

What the pairwise judge changes is the top. In hps-only, paintings got more reliable without getting better. The quality of the good ones added just +0.03 to the group mean, and once HPSv3 saw petals around a centre and a stem, it stopped asking for more pigment. With the judge on, the other half of the story appears. Better here means closer to the pool, so closer to what I rated as "good" or something I liked more. That added +0.12 in judge-led and +0.16 in hps-led, the best of each step rose too, and paint coverage doubled in both runs (0.11 to 0.23, and 0.13 to 0.30) where hps-only barely moved it. With a reference left to beat, a good painting can still get better, and the model starts being rewarded for using more pigment.

It has been revealed that one more finding. The model ignores an explicit instruction, and it is right to. The system prompt asks for fifteen to thirty filled shapes. If we look at the real mean, it is between 7 and 9, and n_shapes barely correlates with reward in any run (+0.000, −0.14, +0.07). The policy is not rewarded for obeying that sentence, so it does not obey it.

There is also a ceiling on the hps-only route. If every rollout matched its good ones, that run's mean would sit at 0.771. Whether more steps would break it is an open question.

The paintings also show something that the tables miss. Within each run, they all look similar. As training advances, the rewards inside each group get closer together, and the median paintings in the opening video look like takes of the same flower. That is GRPO doing what it is designed to do with a pool built from one subject. The pool decides what counts as variety, the same way it decides what counts as quality. If the reward only pays for matching one flower, the model learns to paint that one flower. More diverse output would need a more diverse pool, and building one is more curation work. Surya's newer compositions are an example of this. Alex Yango's animal paintings are the same recipe with different choices in the pool. This is the biggest difference between an aesthetic reward and a maths grader. Behind the number there is a very human job, deciding what belongs in the reward set. Jason Liu's essay on taste says the general version in one line. AI shifted the bottleneck from making to noticing.

Surya closes his blog with some of his favourites. Instead of picking mine, below is a wall with the 178 paintings the reward scored highest across the two judge runs, the same number the reference pool holds, in no particular order. Open it and pick your own.

To choose, you looked at many and kept a few, and that is exactly the job that built the reward of this project. Every painting of every run, with its sketch and its reward, is in the rollouts datasets, and browsable in this gallery.

Since the reward was partly based on my taste, it is fair to close with my verdict as a viewer. To my eye, judge-led is the run that ends up the most diverse and the most artistically interesting. hps-led paints convincing watercolours, but its best ones share a soft, wet-on-wet look that is almost a style of its own. hps-only converges the hardest, and most of its paintings settle on the same colours. You can judge for yourself in the gallery, which has every painting of every run, sortable by step and by reward.

Sources indicate that this project is mostly infra. A run needs a trainer, two Spaces, an inference router and a websocket to stay healthy for hours straight, and every piece that fails quietly turns into a wrong number somewhere else. Half the work is checking that the number you read matches what actually happened.

Failures of the infrastructure were entering the reward as zeros. A render that timed out or a scorer that did not answer scored the same as a bad painting, 0.0 inside the group. Across all my runs that was about 1.5% of rollouts, and in the worst run it reached 5.2%. That trains the model on noise, so those paths now return None and the rollout is excluded from the group.

According to recent reports, I also found a bug in OpenEnv, and sent the fix upstream. The client keeps one persistent websocket, and a socket closed by the far end stayed cached, so every later call failed even though the environment was healthy. It cost me two half-finished runs to find it. The fix is submitted upstream, and the runs launched with it have been running clean since.

Sources indicate that the reward of a step depends on which references it drew. The pairwise judge samples four references per step, so every step faces a different set of rivals, and some draws are simply harder. GRPO itself is mostly safe, because advantages are computed inside the group and a hard draw moves the whole group together. The curve I was reading was not safe, and some of what looked like a bad step was just a hard draw. The image above is one example. Step 12 scored half a point below step 11 mostly because it drew the hardest references of the run, while the paintings themselves look close.

Rounded numbers, and only for the runs that finished.

A step is eight rollouts and takes fifteen to eighteen minutes, of which 70 to 80% is rendering. A single render takes 69 to 96 seconds against a 90 second deadline. Part of that is expected, the Space has no GPU, so Chromium renders the WEBGL canvas in software and p5.brush's bleeds and textures are heavy pixel work. Even so, I expected it to be faster, and I have not found the full cause.

A scorer can cost more than the training that uses it: HPSv3 has to be up for the whole run, so pause the Space, or set its sleep timer, when the run ends.

Everything runs on HF Jobs, with the environment as a Docker Space and metrics in trackio.

Industry observers note that the rule of this project was to reproduce the recipe with every resource open, not to improve it, so a list of untried ideas piled up along the way. These are the ones I would actually try, in order of how much evidence there is.

Multi-step, and letting the model see what it paints. This is the first thing I would try. The original blog trains single turn, so I trained single turn, and in this setup the model paints with its eyes closed. No image ever goes in, and the only feedback it gets is one number. The evidence that a feedback loop works is the pool itself. The reference paintings came from models iterating three rounds under a vision critic, and the later rounds are better. The material that defines the reward was made with a loop the policy never gets.

Smaller models. There is evidence that 35B is more than needed. In my side experiments a 4B already wrote valid sketches that passed the gate. If a 4B can learn this, the cost of the experiment drops by an order of magnitude.

Other ideas on the list are SFT on the pool sources before starting RL, rewarding pigment explicitly, moving the judge's reference mix from easy to hard as the run advances until only love remains, widening the ten-method allowlist for more visual range (my attempts on this crashed more sketches and broke the watercolour look), and checking how consistent the pairwise judge really is by scoring the same image twice.

And the method is not specific to flowers. Alex Yango painted animals with the same mechanism, and Brendan Hogan trained canvas animations against a pool of hand-rated clips. I had also played with something similar before using Simon Willison's pelican benchmark, where code is rendered to an image and scored.

And underneath all of it sits the question this project cannot close. 178 paintings made by models define what this trained model considers beautiful. The pool is the bottleneck, and it is the part of the pipeline with no principled answer.

For anyone reproducing this, there are two deliberate divergences from Narreddi's recipe, both argued earlier in the article:.

In a recent development, the rest, all-linear for the LoRA, infrastructure failures returning None instead of 0.0, stopping the judge runs at step 110, are decisions I had to make along the way because his blog does not specify them. His implementation is not published, so I cannot tell whether they match his choices or diverge from them.

According to recent reports, the per-rollout numbers in this article can be recomputed from the published datasets. Nothing here depends on any Space staying switched on.

Industry observers note that the method and original idea are Surya Narreddi's. The library is Alejandro Campos Uribe's.

Microsoft brings serverless PostgreSQL into Fabric to bridge transactions and analytics

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1011 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • HorizonDB preview follows rivals' moves, with analysts warning tighter integration could make an eventual exit harder.
  • Microsoft has brought its HorizonDB PostgreSQL service into public preview in Fabric, aiming to bring transactional and analytical workloads closer together.
  • The corporation notes applications can submit queries through a single PostgreSQL endpoint, with transactional and analytical work handled by the appropriate engines.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

HorizonDB preview follows rivals' moves, with analysts warning tighter integration could make an eventual exit harder.

Microsoft has brought its HorizonDB PostgreSQL service into public preview in Fabric, aiming to bring transactional and analytical workloads closer together.

The corporation notes applications can submit queries through a single PostgreSQL endpoint, with transactional and analytical work handled by the appropriate engines.

In a recent development, analysts mentioned the move follows similar efforts by Databricks and Snowflake to combine operational databases with analytics. But tighter integration with Microsoft's stack could make applications harder to move elsewhere.

Fabric HorizonDB joins SQL database and Cosmos DB in Microsoft's Fabric database portfolio. "By bringing operational databases, analytics, and AI together on a unified, governed platform, developers can build intelligent applications with less data movement and complexity. Fabric HorizonDB will also serve as the PostgreSQL backend for Fabric apps," Microsoft mentioned.

According to recent reports, microsoft first unveiled Azure HorizonDB in preview in November 2025 and made it generally available last week. It competes with other cloud database services and distributed systems such as CockroachDB and YugabyteDB, both of which support PostgreSQL's wire protocol.

At the time, it said HorizonDB would offer "massive read scale without the need to replicate the database between instances.".

Speaking to The Register last week, Shireesh Thota, veep of Azure databases and Fabric applications, remarked that bringing the system into Fabric – its platform for data lakes, data warehouses, and analytics released in 2023 – would connect operational data in HorizonDB with analytical data in OneLake, Fabric's unified data lake.

"Once the data hits the OneLake storage, you can have analytical engines that take advantage of it. In HorizonDB, the PostgreSQL query engine can talk to the distributed query engine that we use in our Fabric data warehouse. We're fusing these query engines, thereby enabling the developers to submit a query that has pieces of the query that can work on OLTP and pieces of the query that can work on OLAP," he remarked.

It has been revealed that "The application need not worry about two endpoints, or about consistency of data and all that complexity. They can just talk to HorizonDB as a Fabric endpoint, and they can submit all these queries. We are basically operationalizing in OneLake.".

Operational data remains in HorizonDB's database storage, while mirroring maintains an analytical copy in OneLake, introduced in 2023, which replicates a snapshot of the external database to OneLake in Delta Parquet tables and keeps the replica synced in "near real time.".

It has been revealed that thota mentioned the process would not affect the transactional system. "Our core goal is to never impact OLTP workload while we are doing this, and we succeed [by] reading off the log as an additional replica to do this mirroring," he said.

But the overall proposal of putting serverless PostgreSQL OLTP in an analytics platform, bringing it close to OLAP systems, is one some vendors are already executing to meet the demands of latest AI agent-led workloads.

Adam Ronthal, research veep in Gartner's Data and Analytics Group, remarked: "The addition of Microsoft Fabric HorizonDB follows the 2025 acquisitions of PostgreSQL vendors by Databricks – Neon – and Snowflake – Crunchy. It delivers a high-performance, serverless operational RDBMS that is tightly coupled with Microsoft's lakehouse offering and well-suited to the ephemeral demands of AI agents.

According to recent reports, "Competing directly with AWS Aurora and Google Cloud's AlloyDB, HorizonDB acts as a foundational serving layer for the next generation of AI- and analytics-infused applications. For organizations aligned with Azure and Fabric, it provides an industry-standard PostgreSQL foundation for AI development.".

In a recent development, andrew Snodgrass, research vice president of analyst organization Directions on Microsoft, said the announcement of HorizonDB in Fabric was a "surprise," although "a watered-down version" compared to the version of the serverless database that became generally available on Azure last week. "It joins (document database) CosmosDB in Fabric and SQL database (based on the SQL Server engine) in Fabric. It highlights that Microsoft is still focused on making Fabric the data hub of their universe.".

Sources indicate that horizonDB – both in Azure and Fabric – is a PostgreSQL service which Microsoft notes has 100 percent compatibility with the open source system that has enjoyed a meteoric rise over the last decade. The support for PostgreSQL has led some to question the software giant's commitment to its own proprietary OLTP system, SQL Server.

Thota pointed out that the SQL database, based on the SQL Server engine, is already available in Fabric. Microsoft is also evaluating similar integration for that service, although he gave no timetable. "We are just beginning this journey, and most of the innovation is neutral to PostgreSQL and SQL. Some of it would be particular to how the individual query engine fuses with the analytical query engine. PostgreSQL does it slightly differently than SQL, but the idea is that most of the work is neutral. We are evaluating that work as well. I don't have timelines for that, but it is certainly in our thinking," he said.

It has been revealed that nonetheless, Holger Mueller, principal analyst at Constellation Research, said it was good to see Microsoft go all in on support of open source. "In general, it is an acknowledgement that they cannot win the battle for the SQL database with SQL Server – as it is as proprietary as the leader Oracle – and now they bank on the openness of PostgreSQL as another approach," he said.

Industry observers note that however, using HorizonDB integrated into the Fabric/Azure stack may create so many dependencies with Microsoft's technology that lock-in to the vendor will remain a risk. "The primary concerns of open source – scale and support – have been eliminated by Microsoft's commitment and by now track record... the challenges are the embeddings of HorizonDB into the bigger Microsoft stack – which will make portability hard again. But every vendor wants and provides stickiness – clothed in ease of use and lower TCO," Mueller noted. ®.

Introducing Amazon ECS Gateway: A fully-managed ingress solution for ECS services

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (883 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When platform teams manage containerized applications at scale on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), configuring ingress networking for each service often becomes a bottleneck.
  • Today, we’re announcing Amazon ECS Gateway, a newly introduced account-level resource that simplifies ingress networking for containerized workloads by dynamically provisioning and managing the necessary infrastructure on your behalf, with all resources created directly in your account.
  • ECS Gateway introduces a clear separation of responsibilities between platform teams and application teams.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When platform teams manage containerized applications at scale on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), configuring ingress networking for each service often becomes a bottleneck. For every fresh service, teams must provision and connect Application Load Balancers (ALBs), AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificates, AWS WAF web ACLs, and security groups, then keep those resources in sync as services scale, revision, or operate. This per-service overhead slows down deployment velocity and increases the risk of configuration drift across an organization.

Today, we’re announcing Amazon ECS Gateway, a newly introduced account-level resource that simplifies ingress networking for containerized workloads by dynamically provisioning and managing the necessary infrastructure on your behalf, with all resources created directly in your account.

ECS Gateway introduces a clear separation of responsibilities between platform teams and application teams.

Sources indicate that ECS Gateway offers host-based routing using ALBs and enables up to 25 services to share a single ALB, optimizing infrastructure costs. ECS manages the full lifecycle of the underlying infrastructure, provisioning the first ALB when your first service connects, adding more ALBs as capacity is reached, and removing them when no longer needed. Each service receives a unique DNS hostname, giving your teams a ready-to-use endpoint the moment provisioning completes.

Industry observers note that A first look at ECS Gateway In the ECS console, platform team can create a gateway and sets its configuration. The infrastructure role is an IAM role that ECS assumes to provision and manage networking resources such as ALBs, security groups, and certificates in your account. To create a gateway, provide a gateway name and select an infrastructure role. You can optionally associate the gateway with ECS clusters during creation or later.

Sources indicate that choose a load balancing scheme, either public or VPC-internal traffic routing. Under Additional Settings, you can also set up a listener, port, maximum count of load balancers the gateway can scale to, and a web ACL lets you protect your web applications. Some settings, including the name, scheme, VPC, subnets, IP address type, listener protocol and port cannot be changed after gateway creation.

Using AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), call CreateGateway with a name (unique per account), an infrastructure role, and a configuration object. No infrastructure is provisioned until a service connects with a gateway connector.

Once the gateway is created, you can take a look at the detailed configuration, gateway routes, load balancers, and associated clusters.

Now associate the gateway with one or more clusters (many-to-many), to make it available to ECS services on those clusters.

Use AssociateGatewayWithCluster to make the gateway available to services on a cluster:.

Industry observers note that to create and manage the ECS Gateway programmatically, including calling APIs and searching documentation, try the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI coding tool. To learn more, visit the Amazon ECS Gateway documentation.

According to recent reports, ECS Gateway:Behind the scenesA gateway can be associated with up to 10,000 clusters, and a single cluster supports up to five gateway associations. This many-to-many relationship gives platform teams the flexibility to share a gateway across environments or assign multiple gateways (for example, public and private) to a single cluster.

In a recent development, platform teams can control access by choosing which gateways to associate with which clusters. For additional control, use IAM policies to restrict who can deploy services to specific clusters.

Sources indicate that application teams add the gateway connector to each service definition in CreateService or UpdateService. If you have an existing ECS service with its own load balancer, you can adopt ECS Gateway incrementally by calling UpdateService to add a gateway connector. Both ingress paths remain available, allowing you to validate the gateway connection before removing the existing load balancer configuration.

In a recent development, at deployment time, Amazon ECS evaluates the gateways associated with the cluster and connects the service to every compatible gateway. A gateway is compatible when its access type matches the service’s connector filter, it is in the same VPC as the service, and it covers all Availability Zones used by the service’s configured subnets.

Industry observers note that for each connection, Amazon ECS assigns the service to an ALB with available capacity and provisions the per-service resources: an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, a listener rule routing traffic for that hostname to the service target group, and a service security group allowing inbound traffic only from the ALB security group. If no existing ALB has capacity, ECS creates a new one (up to maxAlbCount referring to quota limit). Once provisioning completes, the gateway route becomes ACTIVE, and the service URL is ready to receive traffic.

ECS Gateway handles common operational scenarios automatically:.

Things to Know Here are a few vital details to keep in mind:.

Now available Amazon ECS Gateway is available now in all commercial AWS Regions where ECS is available at no additional charge. You pay only for the underlying infrastructure provisioned in your account when services connect to a gateway, including applicable ALB charges, CloudWatch logs and metrics, ACM certificates, and data transfer charges. To learn more, visit the Amazon ECS Pricing page.

To get started, create your first gateway today in the ECS console, and send feedback to AWS re:Post for ECS or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

Give Your Coding Agents a Memory You Own

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1581 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, I work across several machines, and I switch coding agents depending on the task.
  • In a recent development, earlier this year, Software Forgets: Agent Traces Are the Memory made the case that coding agents already produce the record we keep losing.
  • It has been revealed that while the diagnosis is correct, traces are only potential memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, I work across several machines, and I switch coding agents depending on the task. Every one of them meets my projects as a stranger. The reasoning from “last Tuesday” disappears when the session ends. Each upcoming agent, on each new host, starts from zero.

In a recent development, earlier this year, Software Forgets: Agent Traces Are the Memory made the case that coding agents already produce the record we keep losing. As they search a codebase, try approaches, hit errors, read documentation, and change direction, they leave behind a dense account of not just what changed, but why.

It has been revealed that while the diagnosis is correct, traces are only potential memory. The session logs of an agent are still just an archive. You cannot grep your way to “why did we move off the streaming parser?” across ten thousand turns. For an agent to use those traces while it works, they need indexing, retrieval, ranking, and exact provenance.

That is what funes provides. It is a durable memory layer for your agents (Claude Code, Codex, pi, and Hermes). It is built from the sessions already on your machine. It works locally and becomes part of your agent's normal workflow with one command. When you want it to, it can also travel to a Hugging Face dataset you own, private by default.

Industry observers note that funes is a single binary. Its default inference backend has no ML runtime dependency, and embedding and reranking happen on your machine. Install it:.

That one add command builds the first index, gives the agent recall and get tools, and installs the automation that indexes each completed turn. Indexing is incremental, with latest runs adding new turns rather than embedding the whole history again. The older and deeper content can backfill in bounded steps.

It has been revealed that from there, you just work. When a task touches a past decision, rationale, or finding, the agent can reach for recall itself. You do not need to remember the old session or paste its context into the upcoming one.

With funes added, recall happens inside the conversation. The agent reaches for its memory on its own and names the session behind its answer.

Sources indicate that recall returns the original text, not a summary, and shows exactly where it came from (the agent, timestamp, session, and turn). Each result includes a get command that opens the full turn and its surrounding context.

Underneath, one deterministic pipeline parses every supported trace into the same turn-and-block shape, chunks it, embeds it with a pinned local model, and writes it to a local Lance dataset. A query combines vector and BM25 search, fuses their rankings, reranks the candidates with a cross-encoder, reweights them by recency, and attaches neighboring chunks.

That design gives funes three notable properties:.

The agent as a stranger problem is already solved on one machine. But memory gets more useful when the next agent is running somewhere else.

To make a memory follow your work, bind one when you add funes to an agent:.

The bind publishes your current memory there. funes then keeps it current, indexing each turn locally and publishing at session boundaries. The agent recalls from it throughout. Run the same command on another machine and the memory follows you there.

Underneath, the local memory is a Lance dataset, and the shared memory is a Hugging Face dataset (private by default) you own.

Industry observers note that before anything reaches the Hub, credentials have already been redacted during indexing. Publishing then scans every chunk again and withholds anything that still looks like a secret. The scanner behind this is documented in SECURITY.md, including what it does and doesn't cover.

In a recent development, when an agent reads a remote memory, funes caches the dataset files locally, so warm queries return to local speed. The Hub supplies the ownership, access control, versioning, and distribution it already supplies for other datasets. Your memory does not become an account in a separate memory service, and you do not rent it back through an API.

recall is shaped for agents. When you want to put a question to a memory yourself, use ask. It reads your local memory by default:.

Or point it at a shared memory. We published a memory of funes development, so you can ask why funes works the way it does without creating a memory of your own:.

Industry observers note that funes ask is the read-only, one-question sibling of funes add. It recalls the passages, hands them to a coding agent, and returns a grounded answer that names its sources. It does not install an integration or change the agent's persistent setup.

A retrieval miss is not papered over. If the passages do not support an answer, the agent indicates so. You can rephrase the question or add funes to the agent so it can search the memory iteratively during normal work.

It has been revealed that A shared memory is not tied to the agent or model that created it. Start a task in Claude Code, continue it in Codex next week, and the second agent can recall the first agent's reasoning. Use pi with a local model or one served through the Hugging Face router, then return to Claude.

In a recent development, claude makes a decision; a hook indexes it; Codex recalls it in another session. The older hits in the demo are earlier recordings of the same experiment: an append-only memory remembered the rehearsals too.

This matters in a few different scopes:.

Sources indicate that published memories carry a dataset card and the funes tag, making them recognizable and discoverable on the Hub. The Hub already hosts open weights and datasets. funes adds open working memory. It holds the decisions, failed approaches, and rationale behind a project, queryable by another agent and traceable to the sessions that produced them.

According to recent reports, A long investigation bloats a session until each turn costs more to carry the context than to do the work. The usual answers are to let the agent compact and carry on, or to write a handoff and start fresh. Recall is a third, so we measured them against each other on the handoff-vs-recall benchmark: two tasks whose answer cannot be reconstructed without the session prior knowledge.

Industry observers note that compaction is what most agents do by default, and it was the only one of the three whose result divided: it arrived on one task and never arrived on the other. Where it failed, its summary had flattened the findings that mattered. Recall returns the passages themselves, so a finding does not have to survive summarization.

Recall was the cheapest of the three on both tasks, 8x cheaper than a written handoff on one and 4x on the other.

The lighter segment of each bar is the one-time charge for preparing the channel, the handoff or the compaction, paid before the first question is asked and counted once. A cross marks a channel that never arrives, and so has no cost per success.

“To think is to forget differences, generalize, make abstractions.” — Jorge Luis Borges, Funes the Memorious.

Your agents already wrote the record. funes lives at github.com/huggingface/funes, one command away from turning that record into a memory the next agent can read, on whichever machine you happen to be on.

According to recent reports, funes invents little of this. It leans on open-source embedding models good enough to run locally, on Lance's append-only datasets with cheap incremental writes, and on the Hub's caching and content-dedup for datasets. The work is in fitting them into a memory an agent can actually use.

In a recent development, funes is open source too. Open an issue for anything from an install snag to a recall that missed, or an agent you'd like supported.

It has been revealed that ran funes 1.3.0 on a machine with 19,195 coding-agent sessions already on disk (LongMemEval laid down in the real ~/.claude and ~/.codex layouts), 100 questions whose answer sits in exactly one session, scored by whether that session comes back. Disclosure: I maintain deja-vu, one of the tools in the same table.

Full index: 2h03m on an M4 pro laptop (308k chunks), 6.3s per query. With defaults: hit@1 9/100, hit@5 39, found@50 71. With --half-life 0: 19/46/71 — the 30-day recency half-life halves rank-1 on history older than a month, which is most of what's on a real disk; worth a mention in the docs. Once recency is off, the vector+rerank stack is clearly the best ranker in the table at rank five. The documented one-minute first pass leaves 218 of the 19k sessions indexed (0/100 answered), so the "about a minute" framing is really "about a minute until the embedding job starts".

Industry observers note that for comparison on the same corpus, deja-vu (plain BM25 over 24 agents' files) indexes in 29s and answers in 24ms at hit@1 18/100, hit@5 35. Corpus, drivers and every row: vshulcz.github.io/deja-vu/guide/day-zero.html - happy to be corrected if a setting I missed changes the numbers.

longmemeval does not really need semantic search: BM25 already gives the same ratio you mentioned IIRC, so for this use case this is pretty much expected that it is not worth paying the cost of evaluating the embeddings (this extra cost you see at indexing and recall time). funes shines when the information is actually difficult to find.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meanwhile, Google's homepage demo leaves a familiar button out of the picture.

Microsoft is updating search in its Microsoft 365 Copilot app for owners without a Copilot license, with a toggle to restore the classic interface. Google, meanwhile, is giving AI searches more prominence on its homepage, where the familiar Search button is absent from a newly demonstrated layout.

Microsoft's change is rolling out now and will hit Deferred Release by mid-January 2027. It will impact consumers with a Microsoft 365 license who do not have a Copilot license and "provides modern search controls to help users find, refine, and navigate search results more easily.".

Sources indicate that it's enabled by default, which is a shame since administrators would likely prefer an opt-in rather than opt-out approach, and customers can switch back to the "classic search experience" via a toggle on the search results page. Microsoft has not specified how long this toggle will remain available. Its separate Copilot Search experience had a fallback toggle scheduled for removal 60 days after general availability.

"With the updated search experience, owners can continue to find files using keywords, use modern search controls to refine and navigate results, and search supported connected third-party content when their organization has configured connected sources," Microsoft said.

The results will still only display content to which users have permission. Microsoft advises administrators to brief users and help desks on the changed interface and the option to switch back.

Microsoft's search tweaks arrive as the future of the Google Search button on Google's desktop homepage looks uncertain.

Sources indicate that in a post, Google VP of Product Robby Stein described a collapsible sidebar that lists customers' recent AI conversations, pushing AI deeper into the search experience. Stein called it "a much simpler way to pick up where you left off," and said it would help customers "easily find & jump back into your recent AI searches.".

However, something else was obvious in Stein's post: the Google Search button was not present.

Stein explained in August that Google had performed a "small test on desktop to help people find new things they can do with Search." Part of that test was the removal of the Google Search button.

According to recent reports, users can still submit queries by pressing Enter. Stein said the test would have "no impact to how the core search works.".

It has been revealed that the sidebar rollout doesn't itself confirm the Search button's permanent retirement. For now, its absence from Stein's demonstration is another sign of which features Google wants users to notice. ®.

Latest Update: AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1260 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, we’re announcing the general availability of AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities.
  • Recent findings suggest that using frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models, threat actors can turn a vulnerability disclosure into working exploit code in minutes, and the same tools that speed up development also increase the volume of findings your teams must process.
  • It has been revealed that continuum builds a context graph from two primary sources: your code repositories and your AWS environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, we’re announcing the general availability of AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities. AWS Continuum is a security service that finds and validates code vulnerabilities, then delivers fixes as patches you can automate or as pull requests in your repositories. AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities confirms which findings are exploitable in your environment, ranks the resulting concerns by business impact, and proposes a fix for each one. Every remediation starts in a mode where Continuum proposes the fix and a person approves it before it ships. In the future, you will be able to decide which actions Continuum can take on its own, within the guardrails you define.

Recent findings suggest that using frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models, threat actors can turn a vulnerability disclosure into working exploit code in minutes, and the same tools that speed up development also increase the volume of findings your teams must process. If your organization runs a large application estate, your scanners likely produce thousands of findings a day, and many of them need no action. A finding can be unreachable, unexploitable, or already mitigated by a runtime control. Generic severity scores don’t tell you which resources a threat actor can actually reach, so a critical score on a dev-only utility looks the same as a medium score on a service one step away from a payments database. Previously, confirming whether a finding was exploitable took hours of manual investigation, and shipping a fix with confidence took days of coordination across security, infrastructure, and application teams, because the blast radius of a change is hard to assess without business context. To close that gap, Continuum proves which findings are exploitable and bounds the risk of each fix it proposes.

It has been revealed that continuum builds a context graph from two primary sources: your code repositories and your AWS environment. For AWS, you set up a collector in the account and Region where your code runs. The collector gathers resource details such as AWS Config resources and network configuration so Continuum can judge whether a vulnerability is reachable over the network and what a threat actor could reach from it. From this graph, Continuum learns which systems are business-critical, who owns them, how services depend on one another, and which data each one touches. It uses that picture to identify your highest-value systems, such as customer data stores, payment pipelines, and authentication services, and then ranks each resulting glitch by how close its attack path runs to those systems.

In a recent development, continuum analyzes each finding against your code and its environment context and assigns an evidence level, such as a verdict proven by static analysis of the vulnerable code path. For findings it can reproduce, Continuum runs the exploit in an isolated sandbox and attaches proof-of-concept code with the reproduction steps. It produces the attack path, the supporting source analysis, and a blast radius assessment instead of a risk score alone. It also evaluates whether your existing defenses would detect and stop the validated path.

Recent findings suggest that for each confirmed issue, Continuum generates a fix (a code patch, a dependency upgrade, or a configuration change) and opens it as a pull request in your connected repository, ready to review. Every fix requires human approval: you review and merge the pull request, so the final decision stays with your team. In the future, you will be able to build confidence in specific remediation classes and let Continuum apply those fixes automatically once its confidence gates pass, such as test coverage, scope bounds, and historical success rate.

Recent findings suggest that AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities in actionTo show how this works, I open AWS Continuum in the console and go to Code vulnerabilities. Before I can review issues, I set up an environment. I connect a code source, either a GitHub integration or an Amazon S3 bucket, and then create an environment that scans it on a schedule I choose. An Amazon S3 source has a couple of prerequisites: the bucket sits in the same account and AWS Region where I turn on AWS Continuum, and I grant access through an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role that AWS Continuum assumes. I can optionally add AWS infrastructure context by setting up an AWS Continuum collector in the account and Region where my code runs and authorizing my environment to use it. For the full requirements and steps, see the AWS Continuum User Guide.

The Overview page brings these pieces together in one place, showing my Code integrations, the Environments built on them, and the status of any AWS collector that supplies AWS resource context.

It has been revealed that I open one of my environments. The Problems tab lists validated, prioritized issues rather than raw scanner output, each with a severity, a status, and the time it was created. I choose one of the issues.

It has been revealed that the Overview rates it High severity, with the status Completed and the remediation already Delivered to GitHub. The Risk assessment explains why. Continuum rates its Exploitability as Exploitable, with an evidence level of Static proven and a validation run status of Completed. Likelihood is High, since the service is reachable from an attacker, requires no authentication, and needs no user interaction. Impact is Moderate, which means an attacker gains the ability to modify business data, with a blast radius reaching other owners in the same tenant. A Proof section includes the source analysis behind the verdict.

It has been revealed that the Remediation section demonstrates a fix already delivered as a pull request in GitHub, changing four files, with 50 lines added and 24 removed across the cart service. Continuum opens the fix as a pull request titled Continuum fix, and I choose View pull request to open it in GitHub. The console is explicit that a generated patch does not mean the concern is fixed. I still review and merge it, which keeps the final decision with my team. A Contributing findings section lists the specific scanner finding this issue was built from.

The pull request description carries the same risk assessment, remediation summary, and proof from the console, so whoever reviews it in GitHub sees the evidence without leaving their workflow.

The Findings tab lists the raw scanner findings across the environment, the evidence that issues are built from.

Industry observers note that the Scans tab shows the history of each scan with its status, origin, and request and completion times, and I use Configure scan frequency to change the cadence or Queue scan to run one on demand. The Configuration tab is where I manage the environment: the code and context sources it reads from, its code integrations, environment settings such as whether Continuum creates remediation patches, and the AWS collectors it uses for AWS context.

In a single workflow, I work through the validated issues in priority order with each scan, reviewing the evidence and scope behind each one before I approve and merge the fixes I trust. Every fix waits for my approval, so the backlog keeps shrinking while my team keeps control of what ships.

Sources indicate that now available AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is available today in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon) Regions. For pricing, visit the pricing page.

To learn more, visit the AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities product page and the User Guide. Give it a try in the AWS Continuum console today, and send us feedback through your usual AWS Support contacts.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance. We fine-tune LFM2.5-350M with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using the TRL library and evaluate it on the IFStruct benchmark. The full run takes around 500 samples and 100 training steps, small enough for a free-tier Colab or Kaggle GPU, and is available on GitHub. The results show that even a light fine-tuning procedure improves performance from 22.6% to 29.7% on the IFStruct benchmark.

Structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own. Whether a model reliably returns valid, parseable output in the requested format and shape — schema compliance — is often what decides whether it can be wired into a downstream system at all.

Recent findings suggest that note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog. This notebook doesn't aim to recreate the IFStruct benchmark score, but to show how task-specific fine-tuning of smaller models can improve performance and match that of far larger models.

IFStruct is a benchmark for testing the validity of LLM outputs and schema adherence. The benchmark is open-source in Liquid4All/ifstruct, with the public benchmark dataset available on Hugging Face at LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that our launch post introduced Agent Anomaly Detection, which helps you understand and act on agent behavior that drifts outside its intended boundaries.
  • Agent Anomaly Detection works from an agent's traces and logs, so it doesn't need access to the agent's runtime.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that agent Anomaly Detection is in Private Preview, including monitoring for agents that run outside Google Cloud. To request access, see the Agent Anomaly Detection overview.

It has been revealed that our launch post introduced Agent Anomaly Detection, which helps you understand and act on agent behavior that drifts outside its intended boundaries. It covered agents on Google Cloud, such as Agent Runtime, Cloud Run, and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Many teams also run agents on other clouds: on AWS Lambda next to an inventory database, as a hosted agent in Microsoft Foundry, or on-premises next to a system that can't move. Those agents carry the same behavioral risks, and until now Agent Anomaly Detection couldn't review them.

Agent Anomaly Detection works from an agent's traces and logs, so it doesn't need access to the agent's runtime. If those traces and logs reach your Google Cloud project, it can detect anomalous behavior wherever the agent runs. In this post, we explain what Agent Anomaly Detection needs from an agent on other cloud, then show what it found for an agent on AWS Lambda and an agent on Microsoft Foundry.

Agent Anomaly Detection reads the logging and observability buckets that you choose when you enable it. Telemetry from anywhere works when:.

Agents built with the Agent Development Kit (ADK) for Python, version 2.12.0 or later, can produce this telemetry with ADK's Google Cloud exporters and a few environment variables, which the next section shows.

  • No sophisticated malware or attack framework required.
  • A Romanian hacker, armed with only an open source coding agent, a Chrome browser, and a Mac, tried multiple ways to break into a financial services firm, ultimately found an access key - luckily, it was a decoy - and carried out an entire (almost) attack in under six minutes.
  • Industry observers note that it’s a stark reminder that miscreants don’t need sophisticated malware - as in the Binance heist - or AI pen-testing tools like ARTEX to carry out intrusions into critical networks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

No sophisticated malware or attack framework required.

A Romanian hacker, armed with only an open source coding agent, a Chrome browser, and a Mac, tried multiple ways to break into a financial services firm, ultimately found an access key - luckily, it was a decoy - and carried out an entire (almost) attack in under six minutes.

Industry observers note that it’s a stark reminder that miscreants don’t need sophisticated malware - as in the Binance heist - or AI pen-testing tools like ARTEX to carry out intrusions into critical networks. Open source coding agents, and specifically OpenCode in this case, also work just fine.

“What surprised me most was how little it took and the toolkit: a free coding agent, the curl that comes with every Mac and an ordinary Chrome, all from one laptop,” Jesta co-founder and CTO Lior Finkelshtein told The Register. “Until now I thought that we had more time until tools like OpenCode are used in offensive operations. This incident highlights us that it's already in use in the field, and we will probably see more of that in the future.”.

Jesta is a Tel Aviv-based security startup that builds defensive tools to detect and stop autonomous AI attacks. In a report shared exclusively with The Register, Finkelshtein documented an attempted intrusion targeting a major financial services company that’s also a Jesta customer - the security shop declined to say which one.

Jesta’s investigation into the incident determined that someone in Bucharest downloaded a free AI coding agent called OpenCode and pointed it at the financial services customer on November 16 at 4:24:57 a.m. ET.

According to recent reports, openCode is an open source coding agent that lets owners connect to more than 200 model providers or local models, including Anthropic’s Claude models, OpenAI’s GPTs, Google’s Gemini, DeepSeek, and Z.ai’s GLM. Jesta doesn’t know which model the attacker used, as there was nothing in the traffic that named the model. OpenCode's web fetch tool, however, did name itself, so Jesta knows the attacker used this coding agent - not a scanner - to do the dirty work.

“Nothing in OpenCode was built for hacking,” Finkelshtein said in a Tuesday report about the agent-led attack. But, he added, nothing in the coding agent “stops you from pointing it at someone else's website either. When you do, the agent goes through the site the same way it goes through code. It reads, tries something, reads the result and tries the next thing, for as long as you let it run.”.

That’s what it did in this operation, which took less than six minutes and cost the human operator nothing.

It has been revealed that the first call came from a Chrome browser on a Mac, requesting the front page of one of the financial firm’s systems. The site refused it, and six seconds later, the same IPv6 address in Bucharest, on an ordinary DIGI Romania business line, tried again. It used the same Chrome version, but said it was an Android Pixel 10 phone (it wasn’t) to see if the site would let a phone in (it didn’t).

After failing to gain access through the front page, the agent asked the system for its API definition, which was also refused. Five seconds later, it tried a different address - this one was a decoy set up by Jesta - and it answered the agent, providing the readable file defining how the API works.

The agent read the document, and 13 seconds later followed a link it contained. At 4:26:01 a.m. ET, Jesta’s defenses marked the website visitor as an AI agent, opened a case, and from here on out, everything the agent accessed was contained inside a fake environment designed to trick intruders. This included a phony key, which the attacker then used to attempt to break into the tech giant’s systems.

“It worked like a developer,” Finkelshtein said about the coding agent. “It read the API docs and did what they said. It found a key and used it. It checked whether the lock was real, then made up a key of its own and tried that. None of the threat feeds the customer has knew the address, so a blocklist would never have stopped it. The bar for doing this is now installing an app. Think about how many people can do that.”.

In addition to OpenCode, the attacker used only Chrome 157, both in desktop and mobile modes, and curl/8.7.1, a command-line tool that has shipped with every Mac since macOS 15. The agent passed information between the three tools. It included the planted key in a command-line request and then tested three scenarios – using the decoy key, no key, and a fabricated key – to determine whether what it found in the API documentation was legit.

Sources indicate that it also tried multiple URLs using the browser. While it ultimately identified a valid endpoint, it attempted to read from one that accepts only data submissions, so its request was blocked again. Five minutes and 44 seconds after the first request, it gave up, and the logs haven’t detected any activity from this same intruder since then.

The security shop and its customer disclosed the activity to law enforcement and told us it’s “being handled.”.

While the attacker wasn’t able to steal anything in this attempt, security teams still need to take note, according to Finkelshtein.

Sources indicate that “No blocklist would have helped” detect the malicious traffic, he explained. “Most security tools still decide by asking whether an address is known to be bad, and for this one the answer was no. If that key had been real, it would have been in.”.

Instead of blocklists, Finkelshtein suggests paying attention to what the visitor does. In this case, several of its actions gave it away - including following a link that only existed inside an API doc, using a desktop browser and a fake phone, then curl, all from the same address within minutes, and trying multiple keys - including one with a made up name and then no key - within seconds.

It has been revealed that “Open source lets anyone build software without a major team,” Finkelshtein wrote in the Tuesday blog. “AI is doing the same for hacking. The skill is in the model, the model is a setting, and the person giving the instructions doesn't need to know how any of it works.” ®.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A few weeks ago I presented to a small group of commercial and technology leaders from Brazilian agribusiness at the AWS office in São Paulo.
  • Presenting “GenAI no Agronegócio Brasileiro” at the AWS office in São Paulo.
  • It has been revealed that the rest of the week had a sharper edge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A few weeks ago I presented to a small group of commercial and technology leaders from Brazilian agribusiness at the AWS office in São Paulo. My talk ran through where generative AI fits across the different stages of an agribusiness operation, and the point I kept returning to is that the markets we call traditional are exactly the ones where keeping up with this technology decides who ends up ahead of the curve. Nobody there was arguing about whether AI belongs in agriculture. The questions were about delivery: who receives the output, in which language, on which device, often while driving between farms. That is why a launch I might otherwise have filed under routine leads my list this week. The Amazon Polly Generative engine upgrade added 14 new voices, two of them in Brazilian Portuguese. When your user has both hands on a steering wheel, the interface is a voice.

Presenting “GenAI no Agronegócio Brasileiro” at the AWS office in São Paulo.

It has been revealed that the rest of the week had a sharper edge. The biggest launch is a security service built on the premise that the gap between a vulnerability being disclosed and a vulnerability being exploited has effectively closed, and AWS published the honeypot evidence for exactly that in the same week. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news….

AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available AWS Continuum reframes vulnerability management as an end-to-end job rather than a scanner that hands you a list. It builds a context graph from your repositories and your AWS environment, assigns each finding an evidence level, and reproduces exploitable findings in an isolated sandbox with proof-of-concept code so you see the issue rather than a severity label. It ranks complications by how close the attack path runs to business-critical systems, then opens the fix as a pull request. The control boundary matters: every remediation at the moment requires human approval, so you review and merge the pull request, with autonomous classes of fix gated behind confidence thresholds for the future.

The “why now” came from AWS’s own honeypots in the same week. Amazon Threat Intelligence found a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt in MadPot telemetry dated October 17, four days before CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 were publicly disclosed, and on disclosure day proof-of-concept exploits were circulating around 02:00 UTC, roughly twelve hours before the embargo was due to lift at 14:00 UTC. The practical reading is direct: a patch window measured in days assumes a delay that no longer exists, and an investigation should start from the earliest known exploitation rather than from the disclosure date. AWS also published the AWS WAF mitigations for the same CVEs. Continuum is available in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon).

Industry observers note that introducing Amazon ECS Gateway Amazon ECS Gateway splits the work of exposing a service between the people who own the network and the people who own the application. Platform teams define one gateway with the organization’s subnets, security groups, TLS certificates, listener settings, and AWS WAF web ACLs. Application teams opt in by adding a gateway connector to the service definition, and ECS gives them an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, listener rules, a target group, and a security group that admits traffic only from the Application Load Balancer.

The numbers make the economics clear: up to 25 services share a single ALB, ECS provisions the first ALB on first connect and removes ALBs when they are no longer needed, and a gateway can associate with up to 10,000 clusters, with five gateways per cluster. You can adopt it incrementally with UpdateService while your existing load balancer stays in place. Amazon ECS Gateway is available in all commercial Regions where Amazon ECS is available, at no additional charge.

Last week’s releases Here are some launches that caught my attention this week.

Amazon Polly delivers a major upgrade to its Generative engine – The Generative engine now runs a larger, more expressive catalog: 57 generative voices across 11 languages and 25 locales, with 14 new voices across 9 locales and Hindi and Finnish generally available for the first time. Two of the new voices are Brazilian Portuguese, Leo and Carolina. It is a drop-in upgrade, so the voice names, the same SynthesizeSpeech call, and the price all stay the same while the output gets more natural.

Sources indicate that AWS announces TorchNeuron: native PyTorch support for AWS Trainium (public beta) – TorchNeuron is an open source PyTorch backend that lets you run your model on Trainium by switching to .to(‘neuron’), a configuration change instead of a rewrite, with eager execution and torch.compile intact. It integrates with the Neuron Kernel Interface for custom operators, and it works on Trainium2 and Trainium3 instances. If you want the bigger picture on why hardware choice should not lock in your software, the AWS Insights piece on that theme is a good companion read, and the release lands alongside AWS Neuron 2.33.

Sources indicate that upcoming ways to customize models with Amazon SageMaker AI, without managing GPUs – Training sessions are now generally available, giving you control of the post-training loop, including custom loss functions and reward signals, while SageMaker AI handles GPU allocation, distributed execution, fault recovery, and checkpoint storage. You pay for the tokens SageMaker AI processes, and the meter stops while your reward function scores a batch. There is a full technical walkthrough, the training session APIs, and new support for Muse Glimmer, Qwen 3.8, and Ministral 3.

Recent findings suggest that structured outputs for Claude models available on Amazon Bedrock – You can now get schema-compliant JSON back from any Anthropic Claude model on Amazon Bedrock, across both the bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints, without custom parsing, retry logic, or post-processing. That makes jobs like pulling every required field from a financial report, parsing clinical notes, or routing support tickets by intent far more reliable to automate.

Sources indicate that amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey now supports online migration with zero downtime – You can migrate self-managed Valkey or Redis OSS on Amazon EC2 into ElastiCache Serverless with zero downtime, meaning zero errors returned to the client during the move, measured the way the ElastiCache SLA measures availability. You prepare the migration, start the data sync, then choose a manual or automatic cutover, with no third-party replication tools. It is available in all commercial Regions, the China Regions, and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.

Other AWS news Here are some additional projects and posts that you might find interesting.

Discover tools at runtime with AWS Agent Registry – AWS Agent Registry is a managed catalog for MCP servers, agents, and agent skills, so an orchestrator can search approved capabilities at runtime instead of compiling every tool in at build time. This walkthrough indicates the discover, instantiate, and execute loop in a working sample, with search results that return connection metadata but never invocation credentials.

Recent findings suggest that tokenomics for coding agents: benchmark cost and quality on your own code – Coding assistants replay a growing transcript on every turn, so their cost math is nothing like ordinary inference. This post gives you open source tooling to measure model, harness, and hosting choices on your own repositories and build a cost-and-quality frontier you own, with sample results where routing came out 44.7 percent cheaper for 4.8 percent lower mean quality.

How U.S. Bank migrated 119 TB from Oracle Exadata to Amazon RDS for Oracle – U.S. Bank moved four Oracle Exadata databases totaling about 119 TB to Amazon RDS for Oracle using a config-driven pipeline built on Oracle XTTS, AWS DataSync, and Amazon EFS. The initial baseline copy finished in about 7 days with zero data loss and cutovers averaging roughly four hours per database, over a bandwidth-capped Direct Connect link.

Upcoming AWS events Mark your calendars for these upcoming events.

AWS re:Invent – AWS re:Invent runs November 30 to December 4 in Las Vegas, with more than 2,200 sessions. The session catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so now is the time to build your schedule.

AWS Community Days – AWS Community Day Brasil Norte takes place in Belém on October 31, closing out the 2026 Brazilian community season. Check the hub for events near you.
