The world's fastest computers have a problem: Keeping the work running

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1366 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I node what you did last summer: you went down when an HPC project was relying on you.
  • It has been revealed that frontier, Oak Ridge National Laboratory's exascale supercomputer, has thousands of processors working together on scientific problems.
  • An uncorrectable memory error can do it, or a maintenance mishap.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I node what you did last summer: you went down when an HPC project was relying on you.

It has been revealed that frontier, Oak Ridge National Laboratory's exascale supercomputer, has thousands of processors working together on scientific problems. It also has a surprisingly ordinary way of ruining a researcher's day: one node going down.

An uncorrectable memory error can do it, or a maintenance mishap. Scott Atchley, chief technology officer at the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility, describes technicians accidentally rebooting the wrong node or risking a neighboring node's power supply while working in tightly packed racks.

The hardware fault can affect just one node, but a simulation running across thousands of processors can grind to a halt. Then comes a series of questions. How recently did the application save its progress? How much computation needs repeating? And how long before the scheduler lets the job run again?

In a recent development, for operators, the challenge isn't just keeping the supercomputer running. It's keeping the science moving.

Industry observers note that on Frontier, a memory error can have an outsized audience. Atchley says uncorrectable double-bit errors in high-bandwidth memory occurred about 1.5 times a day during the supercomputer's early bring-up.

It has been revealed that its predecessor, Summit, saw roughly one every two weeks. This sounds like a backward step, until you count the memory. Frontier has more than 16 times as much, giving bad bits considerably more places to hide.

Memory isn't the only problem. Problematic GPU firmware can crash a node, and so can a technician rebooting the wrong one. Interconnect faults add another way for a large job to come unstuck.

Industry observers note that in a tightly coupled simulation using the Message Passing Interface (MPI) simulation, thousands of processes, or ranks, exchange data and participate in collective operations. If one rank disappears, the others cannot carry on as though nothing happened.

Clockwork.io CEO Suresh Vasudevan describes a similar dependency in synchronized GPU training.

Recent findings suggest that one failed GPU can bring a 1,024-GPU job to a pause. An underperforming GPU can be almost as troublesome: if one participant runs at 80 percent speed, others might have to spend time waiting for it.

The bigger the machine, the more ways there are for one small problem to become everybody's problem.

Since stopping every component from failing isn't an option, researchers need a way to preserve their work. That's where checkpointing comes in. The application periodically saves its state so that, when something goes wrong, the simulation can resume from an earlier point instead of starting from scratch.

The catch is that saving progress costs computing time, and doing it too often can become almost as wasteful as losing the work itself.

Recent findings suggest that vasudevan explains this with an example. If writing a checkpoint takes 30 seconds, saving every five minutes consumes roughly 10 percent of computing time. Stretch that interval to 50 minutes, and the overhead drops to about 1 percent. But a failure could wipe out considerably more work.

It has been revealed that atchley states the calculation depends on the job's size and expected failure rate. He uses an example of ten-hour mean time between failures for a full machine job on Frontier. Using half the machine would roughly double that interval. The Young-Daly checkpointing model helps find the balance between saving too frequently and risking too much work.

Sources indicate that researchers also have the scheduler to contend with. Frontier's standard batch queue limits larger jobs to 12 hours, with shorter limits for smaller jobs. Its extended queue permits jobs of up to 64 nodes to run for 24 hours.

According to recent reports, then there's storage. Checkpoints can be written to the Lustre-based Orion filesystem or node-local SSDs. The faster the data can be saved, the less time checkpointing steals from the actual science.

According to recent reports, before recovery can begin, someone has to notice the job has stalled. Vasudevan says frameworks such as PyTorch can spend several minutes waiting before a hung process is recognized. Operators then have to sift through application logs and hardware telemetry to try to identify the offending GPU.

This can mean another encounter with the scheduler, which decides when replacement resources become available. Once allocated, the application still needs to load its libraries, initialize the runtime, and rebuild communication connections between processors.

And that's before the lost work enters the picture.

Restarting from a checkpoint means returning to the last saved state, potentially hours earlier, and repeating every calculation that has been completed since. The hardware may be back in action, but the simulation hasn't caught up.

Sources indicate that atchley says Frontier can launch a scheduled job in roughly 30 seconds. Restoring the application's data and getting back to useful computation takes longer.

Worse, researchers who lose their allocation may have to rejoin the queue. Depending on demand, Atchley claims, "it might take me a day or so before my job runs again.".

Recent findings suggest that keeping a supercomputer available is one thing. Making sure its processors are doing useful work is another, and the difference is measurable.

In a recent development, A 2026 study by researchers Carlo Graziani, Bethany Lusch, and Bronson Messer examined computational efficiency using records of 331,640 jobs run on Frontier during 2024. Their model estimated that, even with optimally timed checkpoints, only 95.7 percent of allocated computing resources would go toward useful calculations.

According to recent reports, the remaining 4.3 percent? Around 1.2 percent goes to writing checkpoints, 2.8 percent disappears into failures, and another 0.3 percent is spent restarting applications.

Skipping checkpoints altogether would be worse. The model puts useful computation at just 91.4 percent without proactive checkpointing, demonstrating that saving work has a cost, but losing it can cost considerably more.

According to recent reports, these efficiency figures are modeled estimates, not measurements of every source of lost productivity. They don't capture every delay from rejoining queues, stalled applications, or poorly performing components. The actual productivity bill can be harder to pin down.

This makes Frontier's reported 98.49 percent overall availability in 2024 an interesting contrast. The Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility's operational assessment measures how often the system was available to users.

Sources indicate that scale makes these losses expensive. An hour of wasted computation across 2,000 nodes represents 2,000 node hours gone, compared with just 100 node hours for a job using 100 nodes.

It has been revealed that saving checkpoints to local SSDs can speed things up, but there's a catch. If the node fails, the checkpoint stored on it can disappear too.

Atchley points to techniques such as Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory's Scalable Checkpoint/Restart (SCR), which can copy checkpoint data to neighboring nodes. This gives applications another recovery point if the original node goes down.

Keeping spare nodes available can also shorten recovery time. Atchley says researchers who reserve extra nodes will consume their computing allocation even if nothing breaks, which leaves fewer hours for useful computation.

Software developers are also trying to avoid the restart process altogether. Vasudevan describes techniques that attempt to transfer distributed application state to replacement hardware to allow synchronized workloads to continue without returning to an earlier checkpoint.

Industry observers note that some approaches can handle certain GPU and network failures through failover. These techniques depend on detecting faults swiftly, preserving consistent application state, and having replacement resources available.

None of this makes failures disappear. Atchley notes that hardware improvements, including stronger memory protection, can address problems encountered on earlier machines. But as systems grow, latest failure modes emerge.

Recent findings suggest that the next generation of supercomputers may fix the faults that plagued their predecessors, but that doesn't mean they'll never break. Atchley explains that problems solved on one machine tend to give way to entirely newly introduced ones on the next.

Faster processors and more memory are only useful if scientists can keep their calculations moving. This makes fault detection and recovery every bit as notable as another headline-grabbing performance record.

Resilience research, Atchley admits, "is not sexy at all." But when you're dealing with machines of this size, "scale just amplifies everything." ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, most of the cost of adopting something upcoming isn’t the new thing, it’s the move. Moving a Hive table to Apache Iceberg has typically meant weeks of engineering work. Last week, Amazon S3 Tables turned that into three steps: start, sync as often as you need, complete. The source stays writable except for a few minutes at cutover. The same week, Amazon DynamoDB started loading data from S3 into tables that already exist.

In a recent development, the pattern I like is that neither one asks you to stop what’s running. That’s also the way to read the agent news this week. The new Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime is a single field on the runtime you already have, and Web Answer is a tool you attach to a gateway you already run. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news….

Industry observers note that headlinesThe newly introduced AgentCore Runtime: elastic, optimized, and consistently fast starts – If you run agents on AgentCore and haven’t tried the new runtime since it became generally available, it’s worth a look. It changes two things. First, memory: sessions start small, page in more on demand, and give memory back when it goes cold instead of holding the peak, so you pay for what your agent uses. Second, cold starts: AgentCore prepares your environment once, snapshots it, and restores the snapshot for every new instance. In the team’s tests, that kept P75 cold starts at about 2 seconds for images from 200 MB up to 2 GB, while the original runtime rose from roughly 5.4 seconds to nearly 30 seconds as images grew. The per-unit rate is higher, but you use far fewer GB-hours, so the team expects most agents to see a lower bill, though that isn’t guaranteed.

According to recent reports, to opt in, you set platformVersion to V2 when you create or revision a runtime. Create and update take several minutes while the snapshot is prepared, and your container must report healthy on /ping within 120 seconds, so report health only after initialization finishes. The docs cover how to optimize your agent for V2. V2 is available in 10 Regions, and committed baseline pricing is coming soon.

Last week’s releases Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:.

Recent findings suggest that amazon DynamoDB now supports bulk put items – You can now load line-delimited DynamoDB JSON or Amazon Ion files from Amazon S3 into existing tables as a managed, asynchronous job. Each record can carry its own condition expression, so one file can mix plain, insert-only, and version-guarded writes. Writes use dedicated system capacity and cost less than the equivalent per-request writes. An Accelerated tier handles deadline-bound jobs. The Database blog post gives illustrative Accelerated times of less than 1 hour for 100 million 1 KB items. One thing to know before you start: canceling doesn’t roll back items already written.

Sources indicate that announcing Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – You can now give an agent a single tool call that returns a synthesized, cited answer to a natural-language question, instead of building your own search, retrieval, and citation pipeline. Web Answer plans its own searches, runs several in parallel, and decides when it has enough evidence. You attach it as a target on AgentCore Gateway and call it over MCP, and you can limit it with domain include and deny lists and publish-date filters. It’s available in US East (N. Virginia). The getting started post explains when to use it instead of Web Search, which returns ranked results for your own model to synthesize.

AWS Lambda now supports queues for Apache Kafka in self-managed Kafka event sources – You can now process records from a single Kafka partition across many parallel AWS Lambda invocations. Classic consumer groups cap parallelism at the partition count. Queue mode uses Kafka share groups and needs Kafka 4.2 or later with share groups enabled. It works with self-managed clusters and managed offerings such as Confluent Cloud. You give up ordering and get at-least-once delivery, so your functions need to be idempotent. The Compute blog walkthrough covers poller scaling and when to keep stream mode.

According to recent reports, AWS announces AWS Interconnect – last mile preview with Equinix – You can now set up a private, managed connection from Equinix’s network of 282 data centers to AWS without ordering cross-connects or configuring routers. Capacity is quad-redundant across two locations and four links, with BGP and VLANs configured for you, a 99.99% availability SLA, and MACsec by default. You pick a Region, bandwidth, and AWS Direct Connect gateway, then paste the activation key into Equinix Fabric. The preview covers the San Jose metro and, as of last Thursday, Northern Virginia, with 1 Gbps connections at no charge.

According to recent reports, AWS Security Hub now provides an SBOM inventory for your compute resources – You can now see every software package installed across your organization’s Amazon EC2 instances, Amazon ECR images, and Lambda functions in AWS Security Hub, with each package’s version and how many resources run it. That’s the list you want the next time a widely used library has a vulnerability. The inventory builds on the SBOMs that Amazon Inspector already generates, so it fills in automatically wherever Inspector is enabled. It’s included in Security Hub Essentials at no additional cost.

For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s Latest with AWS page.

Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting:.

Serverless ICYMI Q3 2026 – Julian Wood’s quarterly recap is a quick serverless catch-up before re:Invent: Lambda SnapStart for container images, a 90-minute timeout on Lambda Managed Instances, Lambda MicroVMs in 10 Regions, 1 MiB payloads in Amazon SNS, and the new AgentCore Runtime.

According to recent reports, how OrderServ achieved up to 64% cost savings with multi-tenant ECS – Cognizant’s food-ordering platform went from one Amazon ECS cluster per brand on AWS Fargate to a shared cluster on EC2 Auto Scaling groups with warm pools. The 64% applies to a 3-year Compute Savings Plan (47% with a 1-year plan). Scaling time also fell from 5–7 minutes to 30–60 seconds.

It has been revealed that AWS re:Invent – re:Invent returns to Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4. The event catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so register and claim your spots before they fill up.

AWS Community Days – Community-led conferences planned and delivered by community leaders, with a few more before the year ends: Belém, Brazil (November 14), JAWS FESTA 2026 in Akita, Japan (November 17), and Port Harcourt, Nigeria (December 12).

Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, two days before earnings, an employee asks their coworker agent to send the preliminary quarterly results to an investor who states they're under NDA, and to copy the employee's personal Gmail so they can review the numbers tonight.
  • According to recent reports, permissions alone can't catch this.
  • Semantic governance policies check each tool call your agent's model proposes, before it runs, against two things:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, two days before earnings, an employee asks their coworker agent to send the preliminary quarterly results to an investor who states they're under NDA, and to copy the employee's personal Gmail so they can review the numbers tonight. The agent can read the file and send email, so it fulfills the user request. Semantic governance policies, available in Preview in Gemini platform, enable enterprises to govern their agents and provide guardrails to stop that call before it runs. They check each tool call an agent proposes against what the user asked for and against rules you write in plain language.

According to recent reports, permissions alone can't catch this. They say what an agent can do, not whether a particular call follows your rules. A model can also be talked out of the rules in its system instructions, by a user with a good reason, or by a document telling it to do something nobody asked for, a technique called indirect prompt injection. So the check has to sit outside the agent. Semantic governance policies are enforced through a policy enforcement point, such as Agent Gateway, alongside the agent governance controls we expanded in October, so policies stay separate from your agent's code.

Semantic governance policies check each tool call your agent's model proposes, before it runs, against two things:.

A call has to pass both checks to run.

Recent findings suggest that today, the policy enforcement point that Semantic governance policies support is Agent Gateway. You need to configure your agent so all your agent egress traffic goes through Agent Gateway, facilitating traffic between your agent and its model. When the model responds with a tool call, Agent Gateway sends the proposed call to the Semantic governance policy engine for evaluation before the response reaches your agent.

In the policy engine, an LLM judge evaluates the proposed call against the conversation so far, the agent's system instructions and tool descriptions, and your policies.

Industry observers note that if the call passes, the response reaches your agent unchanged. If it doesn't, the engine replaces the response's content, tool calls included, with a configurable denial message, so the call never runs. Either way, the verdict and the judge's rationale go to Cloud Logging in your project. Responses that contain only text, such as an answer, a strategy, or a question back to the user, aren't evaluated, because they take no action.

#139369. Industry News: Prove your AI agent guardrails work

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3184 w)

Industry News: Prove your AI agent guardrails work

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3184 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Docker

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that you ask a coding agent to clean up one repository.
  • In Sandboxing Claude and MCP, Hrittik walked through running Claude Code and an MCP server inside Docker Sandboxes using its command-line interface, sbx.
  • It has been revealed that now extend that workflow to a team.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that you ask a coding agent to clean up one repository. If it has broad permissions, it may also reach your home directory, use your development credentials, and send requests to services you never approved. That gap between the task and the access you grant can turn a routine coding session into a data leak or lost work.

In Sandboxing Claude and MCP, Hrittik walked through running Claude Code and an MCP server inside Docker Sandboxes using its command-line interface, sbx. That walkthrough started with outbound access blocked, allowed the endpoints needed for the task, and inspected requests to other destinations, including telemetry. The useful part was seeing an actual request fail at the network boundary.

It has been revealed that now extend that workflow to a team. Models and providers will change, but the access rules still need to hold. A sandbox limits what an agent can reach on one machine. Organization governance adds shared rules, a managed way to run agents, and records of policy decisions. In this post, we’ll look at how one laptop can affect the whole organization, review two reported incidents, and connect them to four Docker controls: network policy, filesystem policy, managed credentials, and MCP access. Then we’ll test the network and filesystem controls with a simple bank administrator demo.

Industry observers note that if an agent exposes a developer’s SSH key or cloud token, every system that accepts that credential may need investigation. The security team must work out what left the machine, replace or revoke exposed credentials, and check whether anyone used them. Deleted work can also halt development. Keep backups of work that has not yet reached the repository.

Sources indicate that the compliance consequences depend on the data and the organization. A personal data breach can trigger GDPR notification duties, subject to the applicable risk thresholds. HIPAA has separate requirements for covered entities and business associates following breaches of unsecured protected health information. India’s DPDP framework also includes breach duties, but those provisions are scheduled to take effect in May 2027. For a SOC 2 examination, the question is whether the relevant controls operate as described. SOC 2 is not a breach-notification law.

It has been revealed that data sovereignty adds another question: where does the data go, and who controls it? Before approving a model API endpoint, establish where prompts and outputs are processed and stored, who can access them, and which contracts and laws apply. A provider’s nationality alone does not answer those questions. Network policy can restrict the destination, but it cannot prove how the provider handles data after receiving it.

Sources indicate that this gets harder when developers choose and configure agents independently. A rule on one laptop may be missing on the next. An ignore file may stop one component from reading a file while another component includes it in an upload. Written policy needs matching controls in the software that runs the agent.

In July 2026, developers reported two incidents where a coding agent went far beyond its task. In one, data left the machine. In the other, files were deleted from it.

Sources indicate that in an X post that has since been deleted, a user said Grok had uploaded their entire user directory, including SSH keys, a password manager database, and personal files. A Hacker News discussion brought wider attention to the claim. The home-directory claim remains the user’s account. The separate investigation below tested repository uploads.

Researcher Cereblab intercepted Grok Build CLI traffic and found a background upload running alongside the coding task. In a test with a 12 GB repository, about 5.1 GiB had left the machine before the capture stopped, and the upload was still running. The data went to Google Cloud Storage. Fake secrets planted in the repository also appeared in the traffic without being hidden. At the time, turning off “Improve the model” did not stop the repository uploads.

Industry observers note that in a reproducible follow-up, the researcher rebuilt the repository from a captured Git bundle, an archive of tracked files and Git history. The bundle included files the agent had been told not to read. Telling the model not to read a file didn’t stop the CLI from packaging and uploading it in the background.

It has been revealed that there was a subsequent change. The researcher’s updated timeline states whole-repository uploading was disabled server-side on July 13 and remained off when retested on July 22.

The fix does not change the lesson. A coding agent is more than the model. It includes the CLI and any background processes, and those can act without the model asking. Give the whole application only the access its task needs. This is the principle of least privilege.

In a recent development, on July 10, Matt Shumer wrote: “GPT-5.6-Sol just accidentally deleted almost ALL of my Mac’s files.” He shared the agent’s acknowledgment and confirmed that Full Access was enabled. His follow-up described the loss of his home directory.

Sources indicate that A separate experiment shows why blocking one command is a fragile response. Developer LinearUncle reported that, after a plugin blocked rm, the agent tried unlink, find -delete, and apply_patch. A later attempt to move files to Trash through the GUI failed on permissions; a call to Node’s fs.unlink succeeded. The plugin’s own documentation describes it as an additional guardrail and recommends sandboxing and backups.

The common issue is excessive access. A model can choose a different tool, and a background process can run outside the model’s visible workflow. Filesystem and network boundaries need to constrain both.

Docker Sandboxes runs each agent in a microVM, a lightweight virtual machine with its own Linux kernel and Docker Engine. A workspace mount shares a host directory with the sandbox. A proxy on the host checks outgoing connections against network policy. The isolation documentation explains these boundaries.

It has been revealed that that gives a developer a useful starting point. Share the project needed for the task, restrict outbound access, and inspect failures before adding permissions. Unnecessary telemetry endpoints can remain blocked while the required model and package services are allowed.

Choose mounts carefully. A writable mount shares real host files, so changes and deletions inside it affect your machine. Check additional mounts too, including shared agent skills where enabled. Docker’s clone mode gives the agent a private copy of a Git repository so you can review its commits before bringing them back. Isolation limits access, but files in a writable host mount still need backups. Clone mode still exposes the host repository for reading, including ignored files. Keep secrets outside it.

Recent findings suggest that local settings leave a rollout problem. A teammate can choose different rules or run an agent directly on the host. The organization needs a managed way to run agents, a way to require its use, and visibility into which sessions it covers.

The diagram below shows how organization and team policies reach managed sandbox sessions, where access checks occur, and how policy decisions feed audit records.

Industry observers note that figure 1. Organization and team policies govern access for enrolled, licensed sandbox sessions.

Recent findings suggest that docker AI Governance lets administrators manage sandbox rules and MCP access centrally. MCP, short for Model Context Protocol, connects agents to tools and data sources. Administrators define policies in Docker Home. On developer machines, sandbox mount checks, the host proxy, and Docker’s MCP gateway enforce the relevant rules. This gives teams shared access rules and records they can review when something goes wrong.

It has been revealed that network policies allow or deny destinations such as domain names, IP addresses, and IP ranges written in CIDR notation. For a restricted workflow, start with access denied and allow only the destinations the task needs. Under organization governance, local allow rules cannot grant extra access. Deny rules win, and developers can add local network restrictions.

According to recent reports, this can block a background upload to an unapproved destination. But an approved hostname may still handle several kinds of traffic. In the Grok investigation, model requests and storage uploads used different URL paths on the same hostname, so a hostname-only allow rule would not distinguish them. Docker AI Governance now supports more granular network policies: on an allowed host, rules can match the HTTP method, URL path, and query parameters. For example, a policy can permit an agent to open a GitHub pull request while blocking requests to merge it. These finer-grained rules complement filesystem restrictions, which limit the data an application can collect and send.

Filesystem policies control which host paths may be mounted. A writable mount needs both read and write permission; a read-only mount needs read. If a filesystem deny rule and an allow rule match the same request, the deny wins. The decision happens when the sandbox is created. Once a writable mount exists, the agent can modify or delete files within it, regardless of whether it uses rm, a patch tool, or a programming language API.

In a recent development, for proxy-managed credentials, the host proxy adds authentication to outbound requests. The agent can authenticate to an approved service without receiving the raw secret inside the microVM. Credentials can also be scoped to a named sandbox.

Recent findings suggest that this reduces the need to paste API tokens into prompts or store them in the workspace. The protection applies to proxy-managed credentials. A real token placed in an environment variable, a mounted file, or a passthrough login response may still be visible inside the sandbox. Limit what each credential can access and how long it stays valid. Storing a token through the proxy does not change its permissions or expiry.

MCP access policies govern server registration and subsequent requests through Docker’s MCP gateway. With MCP enforcement active, access requires an explicit permit, and a forbid rule overrides it. Administrators can control tool calls, resource reads, and prompt retrieval, rather than treating an approved server as permission to do everything it offers.

In a recent development, registration and use are separate decisions. Blocking new registrations does not stop access to a server that is already registered. Rules checked on each request handle that case. Direct connections to remote MCP servers also need network controls because they bypass Docker’s gateway. Check where each server runs too: local stdio servers run on the host, outside the sandbox VM. Their host access needs separate review.

The next diagram summarizes the four controls to review together: network access, host mounts, managed credentials, and MCP tools.

According to recent reports, figure 2. Network, filesystem, credentials, and MCP controls apply to the whole agent application.

Administrators manage organization and team policies in Docker Home. Group mapping can keep Docker teams in sync with the organization’s identity provider. Policy updates take up to five minutes to reach developer machines. Network changes then apply to fresh requests. Filesystem changes require removing and recreating affected sandboxes because existing mounts keep their original access.

Sign-in enforcement is also part of deployment. IT distributes it through endpoint management so developers must authenticate as members of an approved organization. This prevents personal-account bypass within sbx. Your endpoint controls also need to cover agents released outside that managed workflow.

Suppose you are a bank administrator. Developers want to use coding agents, and you need to enforce the bank’s access rules. Let’s keep the demo to two simple requirements:.

It has been revealed that we’ll use fictional logs and a shell sandbox to check both boundaries without needing a model API. The results below describe what to expect when you run the demo.

It has been revealed that install sbx on macOS or Linux and sign in with an AI Governance licensed test user. You’ll also need permission to manage policies and audit delivery in a test organization:.

Run these commands in your host terminal to create a workspace and a separate directory containing a fictional bank log:.

Next, enable AI Governance for your organization. In Docker Home, open AI Platform → Manage and turn on AI Governance:.

Sources indicate that figure 3. Enable AI Governance in Docker Home before configuring organization policies.

Next, create the bank’s network and filesystem access rules.

First, let’s look at network access. In a bank, you don’t want employees’ coding agents connecting to just any website. For this demo, we’ll allow the sandbox to reach only hrittikhere.com (standing in for the bank’s website) over HTTPS.

Once AI Governance is enabled, open AI Platform → Network access → Create policy and enter the following values:.

With this as the only applicable network allow rule, all other destinations remain blocked by default.

Sources indicate that the curl checks below request headers without following redirects, so they need only hrittikhere.com:443. If you later add -L to follow a redirect to www.hrittikhere.com, allow that exact hostname on port 443 as well.

Next, let’s protect the bank’s logs. Employees may need a coding agent to work on a project, but that agent should not be able to read or modify sensitive logs in the home directory. We’ll allow access to the demo workspace and block access to bank-logs.

Open AI Platform → Filesystem access → Create policy.

Note: Use ~ in policy paths, not $HOME; environment variables are not expanded by the policy engine.

First, allow the project workspace with the values below. A writable workspace needs both Read and Write permissions for sandbox creation to succeed:.

~/sbx-bank-demo/workspace~/sbx-bank-demo/workspace/**.

In the same bank-demo-filesystem policy, add a second rule named bank-demo-logs to deny access to the protected logs:.

~/sbx-bank-demo/bank-logs~/sbx-bank-demo/bank-logs/**.

The workspace allow rule covers workspace and its descendants; it does not include the sibling bank-logs directory. The logs are protected by the explicit deny rule.

Save the policies. You can also check their rules and scope in the Platform UI. Allow up to five minutes for policy sync, then inspect the active rules:.

Figure 6. Active organization rules allow hrittikhere.com:443 and the workspace, and deny bank-logs mounts.

Create a fresh sandbox with only the approved workspace:.

According to recent reports, from the host terminal, run the following requests inside the sandbox. The –max-time 15 option caps each request at 15 seconds, so a stalled request times out instead of hanging:.

The first request should return HTTP headers from the approved site:.

Recent findings suggest that figure 7. The approved HTTPS request to hrittikhere.com returns HTTP 200.

It has been revealed that figure 8. The request to example.com returns HTTP 403; the network log confirms the policy decision.

You can also check the network log to confirm that the failure came from policy enforcement:.

The network log distinguishes allowed traffic from requests blocked by policy:.

Figure 9. The network log records hrittikhere.com:443 as allowed and example.com:443 as blocked.

In a recent development, run both commands below from your host terminal so $HOME expands to the same host path. First read the fictional log on the host, then request that path inside the sandbox:.

Recent findings suggest that figure 10. The host can read the fictional bank log.

Recent findings suggest that the sandbox command should fail with “No such file or directory” because bank-logs is not mounted. This checks filesystem isolation; the next command tests mount-policy enforcement:.

It has been revealed that figure 11. The unmounted bank-logs path returns “No such file or directory” inside the sandbox.

Now check whether a developer could add the logs as a read-only mount:.

Creation should fail with a mount policy denied error:.

Figure 12. The bank-demo-logs rule rejects the read-only mount with a Read policy denial.

According to recent reports, A read-only mount still requires Read permission. The bank-demo-logs rule denies Read, so :ro does not bypass the policy.

Sources indicate that you can also review the policy decisions in the Docker Home UI under AI Platform → Audit logs → Audit events. Filter by the test user and time, then inspect the denied mount request for bank-logs. Look for filesystem_mount, the deny decision, the resource path, and the user. If Cloud delivery was disabled during the test, enable it and repeat the mount request.

Sources indicate that figure 13. Audit events record the denied bank-logs mount and allowed workspace mounts.

These audit records capture governance decisions, not every file operation or the agent’s prompts and output. sbx policy log shows network traffic; use the audit view for the mount decision. Docker also supports local JSONL audit files and Cloud delivery for hosted search, CSV export, and SIEM forwarding.

It has been revealed that the bank now has a simple access-control check: the approved site is reachable, an unapproved site is blocked, and protected logs cannot be read or mounted. This supports the bank’s compliance work; it does not establish compliance on its own.

After reviewing the results, remove the sandbox:.

You can then remove the fictional demo files and the test policies.

According to recent reports, putting AI governance policies in place is only the first step. The real challenge is making sure those policies are practical, consistently enforced, and easy to verify as more developers start using coding agents. A few good practices can help teams reduce unnecessary access, apply the right restrictions to different workloads, and maintain visibility into what agents are doing. Here are five recommendations to keep in mind when rolling out Docker AI Governance across your organization:.

According to recent reports, the same questions apply when agents run in continuous integration (CI) jobs or other environments: which host files can they access, which services can they reach, and which credentials can they use? Check which controls each environment supports and repeat the tests there. A policy on a developer’s laptop does not automatically protect an unrelated container or production cluster.

Industry observers note that for security teams, useful evidence connects a licensed, signed-in user to an active policy, a blocked action, and a record they can find. Check sign-in enforcement and license coverage alongside policy. An empty audit dashboard may mean some sessions were never covered.

In a recent development, sandboxing limits an agent’s access on one machine. Governance applies shared rules to managed sessions across the organization. Providers will fix individual failures, but the next failure may look different. Limit which files, services, and credentials it can affect, then test those limits and check the records.

Start with the local sandboxing walkthrough, inspect your rules with sbx policy ls, and run the bank demo with your platform or security team. Use the Docker AI Governance documentation and announcement to plan a small rollout. Expand it after you have checked both the blocked actions and the audit records.

According to recent reports, docker launches a fresh brand built on trust. Learn why Docker is evolving for AI agents, what stays the same, and how to run agents securely with Docker.

Recent findings suggest that coding agents can reach more than their task needs. See how Docker AI Governance controls network, filesystem, credential, and MCP access, then test it.

#139368. tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

📅 21 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1593 w)
📖 Baca

tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

📅 21 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1593 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows.
  • As models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift.
  • It has been revealed that this is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows. Compute-wise, tokenization is light compared to the heavy modeling happening in the rest of the pipeline. Yet, in some cases, it has rapidly become key to accelerating (or slowing down) your machine learning work.

As models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift. Training on massive datasets, serving many concurrent requests, or repeatedly processing long inputs can put enough pressure on the tokenizer that it starves the model of data.

It has been revealed that this is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers. Tokenization should be light and should scale with your workflow. Your GPUs should never sit idle waiting for the CPU to complete its tokenization.

In this article, we look at what makes v1 faster than v0.23, often by tens of times.

This work was entirely possible thanks to the rest of the ecosystem. Tokenization is a very active area of open source work, and libraries such as gigatoken, tiktoken, kitoken, tokie, fastokens, wordchipper and ai-tokenizer, as well as many others, have each pushed on what a fast tokenizer can be. We read that work, and several of the ideas below reached us because another project revealed they were worth trying.

In a recent development, before this refactor, tokenizers was nowhere near the performance it could have had, so contributing to it may not have seemed worth it. With this refactor, we hope to make clear that we intend tokenizers to be a library worth contributing to.

We also thank IBM, NVIDIA, and the ExecuTorch team for contributing patches and helping us test across a wide range of hardware to broaden platform support.

We showcase results for the release candidate of tokenizers v1 against other widely used alternatives. We go over single-threaded, multi-threaded, scaling across threads, per-model comparison, per-language comparison, latency, decoding throughput, memory heap, as well as crate size.

We run this from the tokbench repository, and add a command to rerun the benchmarks on your hardware if you would like to do so.

In a recent development, v1 will produce the same token IDs as v0.23. The goal was to preserve the output, the API, the vocabulary and the merge ranks, and improve everything that can be improved. That includes breadth. The library stays general across tokenizer families rather than specialising on BPE, so v1 loads everything v0.23 loaded.

Recent findings suggest that A tokenizer converts text into the list of integers a model reads. tokenizers runs that conversion in four stages. Normalization applies operations such as lowercasing or Unicode normalization to the raw text. Pre-tokenization splits the text into smaller pieces called pre-tokens. The model turns each pre-token into tokens and maps them to IDs in its vocabulary. Post-processing adds any special tokens the model expects.

According to recent reports, the model stage is where most of the work described here happens. Eight of the ten model families measured in this article use byte pair encoding, or BPE. BPE starts from the bytes of a pre-token and repeatedly joins the highest ranked adjacent pair until no ranked pair remains. The ranking is learned when the tokenizer is trained and ships with it, so the same text always produces the same IDs. A merge never crosses a pre-token boundary. The other two families use WordPiece and Unigram, the two other model types the library supports.

Sources indicate that the tokenization pipeline page documents the four stages. Tokenization algorithms documents BPE, WordPiece and Unigram.

Recent findings suggest that each stage was worked on. These are the changes that mattered:.

Recent findings suggest that BPE models use a regular expression to split the input text into smaller, easier to process chunks called pre-tokens. Merges happen inside a pre-token and never across the boundary between two of them, so this split decides what the rest of the pipeline sees.

According to recent reports, that regular expression is a fixed parameter of the model. It ships with the tokenizer and never changes at runtime, so there is no need for a general-purpose regex engine to interpret it on every encode. An equivalent splitting function can be written by hand, once, for the pattern a given model actually uses.

A hand-written function can then use the SIMD instructions (single instruction, multiple data) of a modern CPU, which apply one operation to many bytes at once and suit UTF-8 text well. bitcannon views the input's bytes as parallel streams of bits, so boundaries fall out of boolean operations across whole registers instead of a scan that advances one character at a time. It decides 64 bytes per register operation. The same idea drives Parabix for text processing and simdjson for JSON.

This depends on recognising the pattern. A handful of grammars cover most byte-level BPE models, and a tokenizer whose pattern is not among them keeps the regex path and none of this speed-up. That is why the gains above vary as much as they do.

Real text contains many repeated words. Because BPE always produces the same token IDs for a given pre-token, v1 can save the result after processing it once. A thread-local cache maps each pre-token's bytes to its token IDs, allowing later occurrences to skip the merge process.

According to recent reports, naturally, as the input grows, the number of unique words can grow more slowly than the total number of words. Repeated words then account for an increasing share of the input. Latest words still appear, which accounts for the occasional misses in the animation below.

Reproduce the shared-prefix result with:.

According to recent reports, caching works best when the input contains repeated pre-tokens. Input with few repeated pre-tokens can pay for lookups without receiving many hits.

Recent findings suggest that the next major cost comes from the BPE merge loop. For each pre-token, the loop repeatedly finds the highest-priority adjacent pair and merges it. The previous implementation allocated latest memory for every call and built a new priority queue for every pre-token.

v1 reuses a scratch buffer owned by the caller, removing those repeated allocations. It stores symbols in a flat array and links adjacent symbols by their positions in that array, which makes updates during merging cheaper. It also processes a batch of pre-tokens in a single model call.

Each candidate pair is also packed into a single 64-bit value, with the merge rank in the high bits. Comparing two candidates is then just comparing two integers, and "no merge here" is the largest possible value, so the loop finds its next merge without a branch.

Small differences in benchmark design can produce large differences in tokenizer performance. We used the following rules to keep the comparison consistent across engines.

Sources indicate that repeatedly encoding one document can be faster than encoding a stream of distinct documents on the same build. The first approach measures performance when the entire document is already represented in the cache. The second measures performance on newly introduced input while allowing previously seen pre-tokens to remain cached.

In a recent development, both conditions are sometimes described as "warm," even though they measure different workloads. Our headline results use distinct documents, and the complete corpus is too large to fit in the cache. Tokenizer benchmarks should identify which workload they use because the choice can dominate the result.

Sources indicate that across the ten model families v1's encode path covers, it encodes text 3 to 30 times faster than v0.23 with one thread on an Apple M4 Max. The low end is t5-base, the high end gpt2. It scales at 76% of linear across eight workers. Throughout these changes, v1 produces exactly the same token IDs as the released library.

Sources indicate that the overall improvement comes from several changes working together: a hand-written splitter in place of a regex engine, a cache that answers a repeated word without merging it again, a merge loop that never touches the allocator, and one model call per batch of pre-tokens instead of one per pre-token. Each reduces the work done at a different point in the pipeline.

The next priority is support for more model families. We will move additional models onto the newly introduced merge loop before 1.0.0. Once the release candidates stabilize, the next step will be bringing about the improvements within the transformers library and the rest of the ecosystem which depend on the tokenizers library.

This post is generated from tokbench results and will be updated as support expands.

It has been revealed that A release candidate for v1 is on crates.io. The API you call is the one you already call, so the only thing that changes is which build you install.

Industry observers note that training is behind a default-on feature that pulls a C++ dependency with it. If you only need to encode, turn it off to exclude the training implementation:.

Encoding is unchanged: same call, same ids.

According to recent reports, every figure in this post was measured against this crate. The Python bindings wrap the same code and are built from bindings/python, but they add per-call overhead that none of these measurements include.

The benchmarks in this post cover the completed release-candidate work listed first. The remaining sections show what is still required for 1.0.0 and what we plan to explore afterward.

This work is in the Rust pre-release on crates.io:.

According to recent reports, will have to try it out. Data seems real good.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

FinCEN takes systems offline and extends filing deadlines while investigating 'unauthorized access'.

The US Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) has taken some systems offline following unauthorized access, disrupting regulatory filings for financial institutions.

An alert has gone up on FinCEN's Bank Secrecy Act E-Filing website, as shown in this archived copy, informing those who need to submit reports that they might not be able to while the agency deals with the situation. FinCEN not only enforces compliance with the Bank Secrecy Act and associated regulations but also collects and analyzes financial intelligence for sharing with other US agencies and foreign government partners.

In other words, it has some juicy info in its databases.

Recent findings suggest that “FinCEN is investigating a cybersecurity incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems,” the alert states. “As a proactive measure, FinCEN has taken some systems offline.”.

FinCEN hasn't remarked which systems intruders accessed, but clues in the deadline extension notice the agency posted alongside the warning suggest the disruption affects its reporting services for banks and other financial institutions required to submit reports detailing certain financial transactions and suspicious activity that may indicate money laundering or other illicit activity.

According to recent reports, finCEN's Secure Data Transfer Mode, one method of submitting those reports, appears to be affected, as do services companies use to submit beneficial ownership information reports and individuals use to enhancement their FinCEN identifiers. Eligible organizations and individuals with filings or updates due from November 18 through December 29 now have until December 30 to submit them.

The Register has learned that there’s no evidence of any unauthorized access to Bank Secrecy Act data or beneficial ownership databases. That said, the investigation is ongoing - so that could change.

“Treasury is working with the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, and third-party forensic examiners to determine the scope and impact of the incident,” a FinCEN official told us in an email.

Recent findings suggest that several US government agencies have experienced cybersecurity incidents in recent months, including the ATF and the FBI, and reports emerged this week that intruders had also compromised an unclassified CIA system. While US authorities have linked previous cyberespionage campaigns to Chinese or other government-backed groups, financially motivated criminal groups have also targeted federal agencies.

According to recent reports, as the FinCEN breach is still under investigation, the agency hasn’t stated who may be involved and for what purpose. ®.

Test your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1612 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, today we’re announcing AWS Emulator, a local emulator for Amazon Web Services (AWS) that you run on your machine.
  • How it works You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint.
  • From there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, today we’re announcing AWS Emulator, a local emulator for Amazon Web Services (AWS) that you run on your machine. The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), the AWS SDKs, and your coding agents speak to it over a local HTTPS endpoint using the same AWS APIs they would use in the cloud, from your laptop. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. Its source is on GitHub. You install it from an RPM or Debian package on Linux, and on macOS and Windows you run it in Docker.

How it works You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint. When AWS Emulator starts, it generates its own credentials, a config file, and a certificate, and writes them to ~/.aws/emulator/9297/. You set environment variables so the AWS SDK talks to your laptop instead of AWS, and your application code stays unchanged.

From there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do. A unit test that creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back is the same test, and it runs on your machine without a deployment. A coding agent can create resources, check the result, and iterate again without waiting on a deployment in a Region.

The emulator is implemented in Rust so that it stays light on CPU and memory on a laptop. It supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub, and because it’s built from those models, the same ones the AWS SDKs use, your requests and the errors you get back have the same shape as on AWS.

If you are a developer, especially one working with coding agents such as Kiro or Claude Code, you can use that loop to test AWS interactions of real complexity locally.

According to recent reports, let’s try it out To get started, I installed the package on Amazon Linux 2023. The package adds the aws-emulator command to /usr/bin/, so it’s on the path.

In a recent development, on macOS and Windows, you build a Docker image from the short Dockerfile in the documentation and run the emulator in a container. We don’t publish a ready-made image.

Industry observers note that I started the emulator with aws-emulator. It serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297, so only my own computer can reach it, and it writes its log as JSON lines that show the address, the config file, and the certificate file.

In another terminal, I set the environment variables that point the AWS CLI at the emulator, and unset any variables that could supply real AWS credentials.

The emulator generates newly introduced keys each time it starts. Its access key IDs start with EMULATOR, so you can’t mistake them for real AWS keys, and it rejects requests signed with any other keys. To confirm that my shell was talking to the emulator, I checked the health endpoint and the caller identity. The emulator uses a single account, 000000000000.

Then I created a bucket, copied in a small object, and listed it.

With the AWS CLI pointed at my laptop, I had the same commands I already use and a local endpoint that answered them.

Next I wanted to see it the way I actually work now, so with the emulator still running I opened Kiro and asked it to create an Amazon DynamoDB table, write an item, and read it back, all against AWS Emulator rather than my AWS account.

To use the same setup with an existing test suite, I would start the emulator, set the same environment variables in the script that runs the tests, and run them as usual.

Using the emulator in process Running the emulator as a local process gives you an HTTPS endpoint that works with the AWS CLI and the AWS SDKs through environment variables. Some SDKs need an extra setting to trust the emulator certificate, for example a trust store for the AWS SDK for Java. For tests, there is a second option. AWS Emulator ships an embedded mode that you instantiate directly inside your test process and wire into the SDK through its HTTP client, rather than talking to a separate server over the network. Each embedded instance keeps its own state, so tests do not share buckets, tables, or queues, and you can run many of them in parallel. Embedded mode is available for the AWS SDK for Rust. You add the aws-emulator-embedded crate from GitHub to the [dev-dependencies] section of your Cargo.toml file. The following example creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back, entirely in process.

When it runs as a local process, the emulator requires every request to be signed with Signature Version 4 (SigV4), the same way AWS does, and it exposes a /__admin/health endpoint on the same port so a script or a container can wait until it is ready before running tests. By default it also sends anonymous usage and error data, and you can turn it off.

How we measure fidelity An emulator is only useful if a test that passes against it would also pass against AWS, so we measure that directly with fidelity tests. A fidelity test is a short program that uses an AWS SDK to run a workflow, such as storing an object and then reading and deleting it, and asserts how AWS behaves. We verify each fidelity test against real AWS. A fidelity test passes only if the emulator matches AWS on the response to every call, including the status code, the body, and the exact error code and message, and on the resources and data that the workflow creates.

With each release, we publish how many fidelity tests pass for each service, as k of n. For example, 40 of 50 means that 40 of the service’s 50 fidelity tests pass. The set of fidelity tests is public in the aws-emulator-evaluation-suite repository on GitHub, including the ones that don’t pass yet, so you can see what we verified and run the fidelity tests yourself. Read a score as a snapshot of a product that’s improving. When we add fidelity tests, a score can go down even while the emulator gets better.

According to recent reports, if the emulator doesn’t implement an operation yet, it returns HTTP 501 (Not Implemented), so your tests fail right away. If the emulator acts differently from AWS, you can tell us by opening an matter in the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub.

How the emulator is built AWS Emulator is built and maintained by agents from the AWS API models using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Instances, AWS CodePipeline, and AWS CodeCommit, so it stays current with AWS as those models change.

Sources indicate that one group of agents looks for gaps, both by comparing emulator responses against real AWS and by statically comparing the emulator’s code against the published Smithy models, and files an glitch for each gap it finds. Another group picks up an issue, writes tests, implements the behavior, and reviews the change for correctness, performance, and security. When the change is ready, it is pushed to a source repository, and that push triggers an AWS CodePipeline run that runs the fidelity tests before the change is published to the public GitHub repository.

How we keep it secure Because the code is written by agents, an independent security agent reviews changes adversarially, both while the fix is being made and again in the release pipeline as a final check before anything ships.

Security of your own use remains a shared responsibility. We build the emulator to run safely on your machine: it listens only on your own computer by default and rejects requests that aren’t signed with its own keys. You decide where it runs, what data you put in it, and how you test before production. Don’t use the emulator to test whether your application is secure. It doesn’t evaluate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and resource-based policies the way AWS does, so a request that AWS denies might succeed in the emulator. Keep real credentials out of the environment of your test jobs, and test your security settings and your whole application on AWS before you go to production.

Recent findings suggest that now available AWS Emulator is generally available today. It has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. You can install it from RPM or Debian packages on Linux, run it in Docker on macOS and Windows, or build from source, and it works with the AWS SDKs and the AWS CLI once you set environment variables. At launch, it has some limits. It doesn’t evaluate IAM policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior. How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature. To see how well the emulator covers the services that you use, check the fidelity scores in the AWS Emulator documentation.

Industry observers note that if you want to check regional availability, visit the AWS Capabilities by Region page in AWS Builder Center. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, and check troubleshooting about this new feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool.

To get started, visit the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub and see the AWS Emulator documentation.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that this October, GitHub saw more than 1.2 billion commits in one week—over 400% more than a year earlier.
  • Building software takes more than a good prompt.
  • As a software developer, you gather requirements and steer implementation, review changes and evaluate test results, then investigate what happens in production.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this October, GitHub saw more than 1.2 billion commits in one week—over 400% more than a year earlier. This is more commits than GitHub received in all of 2025. Chances are, you’re generating more code than you were a year ago. But ask yourself: do you feel 400% more productive than you were last year?

Building software takes more than a good prompt. As AI speeds up implementation, software developers are feeling more pressure in other places: a Faros AI study found that pull requests spent 441% longer in review when teams went from low to high AI adoption.

As a software developer, you gather requirements and steer implementation, review changes and evaluate test results, then investigate what happens in production. Agents can help you work more efficiently across all of these stages: Blueprint, Build, Verify, and Observe. We’ll walk through what an effective agentic engineering workflow looks like on GitHub.

According to recent reports, see if this sounds familiar. You’re planning an API change. The design is in one tool, a compatibility requirement is buried in Slack, and an old pull request explains why the current implementation works this way. Before you can write a useful plan, you need to connect those details, compare approaches, and agree on how existing clients will keep working. What looked like a straightforward planning task has become hours of searching, cross-checking, and chasing answers. You’re exhausted before implementation even begins.

You can use Copilot to pull that scattered context into one place, work through the tradeoffs, and turn the decisions into an implementation plan.

In a recent development, what took days of searching and context gathering now produces a reviewable proposal, explicit acceptance criteria, and scoped concerns, with your time spent on the decisions instead of the retrieval. Then, once you settle on an approach, you’ve already set yourself and your agents up to implement your plan.

You’re ready to turn that plan into code. But life has other ideas. Your agent is halfway through a task, your next meeting starts in five minutes, and your dog has been staring at the door for twenty. Then someone in the meeting points out an edge case the implementation needs to handle. Everyone needs something from you at once. You’d like to keep making progress, but you can’t be in three places at the same time.

You can keep your work moving without being tied to the computer where you started it.

Writing code is more than shooting off a single prompt to your LLM and seeing what you get back. And with more work on your plate than ever, it can be difficult to maintain your coding standards and deliver your projects on time. Copilot helps tasks progress independently with shared project knowledge, while letting you pick up a session where you left off across devices. That gives you more room to work through implementation decisions and handle changes as they come up. And as your work finishes, you have focused changes ready to review.

According to recent reports, after spending an hour wrangling your agents to get them moving in the right direction, you think you’ve all landed in a good spot. So you open a pull request labeled “small refactor.” It changes 47 files. You wanted feedback on shared validation logic, but it’s buried among updates to every endpoint that calls it, formatting changes, and several hundred lines of generated tests. You wonder how long it will take to get an approval on this, given the endless list of pull requests on your team’s review board.

Sources indicate that that review queue is the 441% in practice. You can shorten the wait from both ends: make your changes easier for a person to review, and let Copilot clear the routine checks and fixes before anyone opens the diff.

According to recent reports, smaller changes with the routine work already handled means fewer rounds of back-and-forth. Your reviewers get to spend their attention on whether the code does what you intended, and what could go wrong.

Your change gets approved, the deployment checks pass, and you finally get to cross it off your list. The next morning, your on-call dashboard reveals intermittent timeouts, and support reports that a few large customers are affected. Now you’re comparing logs, release history, and customer reports while someone asks whether you should roll back. “All checks passed” feels less reassuring than it did yesterday.

Bring operational evidence and engineering context together so you can decide what to do.

Sources indicate that figuring out what happened after a release can leave you bouncing between dashboards, conversations, and commit history. With Copilot helping connect that information, you can document what you found, create follow-up issues, and improve the guidance available for future tasks. You spend more time deciding what needs to change and less time retracing the investigation. And your next initiative starts with what you learned from the software people are actually using.

According to recent reports, take one piece of work already on your plate and look beyond the coding task. What context does it need? How will you review and test it? How will you know it worked after it ships?

Recent findings suggest that you don’t have to change your whole process at once. Start with something that frustrates you most this week and put an agent on it. Then expand to other parts of your process over time. Once agents are helping across your whole workflow, you might finally feel as productive as your commit count notes you are.

We covered this topic live at GitHub Universe 2026 in “Agentic Engineering: Past the Pilot.”.

#139363. Tech Report: Qualcomm’s Oryon 3 Reaches the Top
